summary: Brosmer made his way to Minnesota after a successful career at New Hampshire, following his recruitment as a zero-star prospect out of high school. He doesn’t possess above-average NFL arm talent and will struggle to truly threaten defenses with his arm, though he does have decent zip on passes up to 30 yards. His lack of NFL height is noticeable when throwing over the offensive line, particularly over the middle of the field—there are reps where he’s visibly throwing on his tiptoes. However, he is generally a good decision-maker, especially in 2024, as he kept the ball out of harm’s way and avoided unnecessary sacks. His quick footwork and fast release allow him to navigate pressure well within the pocket.
pros_and_cons: Crisp footwork in dropbacks. Fluid, high-paced movements let him react quickly to pressure. Tough quarterback who can absorb contact. Displays decent zip on short and intermediate throws. Generally makes smart decisions with the football. Smaller-than-ideal frame, especially for a QB with limited mobility. Struggles with consistency under pressure. Arm strength is below average to average by NFL standards.

summary: Dart is a former four-star quarterback recruit who was not only a record-breaker on the gridiron—throwing 67 touchdowns to just four interceptions as a senior — but also a two-time all-state baseball player as a third baseman. He began his college career at USC but transferred to Ole Miss after Lincoln Riley brought in Caleb Williams. A natural athlete and solid playmaker, Dart has earned an elite passing grade over the last two seasons. His playing style is enticing — he is light on his feet in the pocket, capable of slipping sacks and possesses a decently quick release. His arm strength appears average by NFL standards. He is too comfortable throwing off his back foot, even when not under pressure. While his tape shows plenty of deep throws, his ball placement on those attempts leaves more to be desired. He is experienced in throwing concept routes that put a single defender in conflict (e.g., slant-flat, curl-flat, smash) but lacks anticipation when making full-field reads. His mobility is solid, and he is best suited for a shotgun-based system, having taken just eight snaps under center over the last two seasons.
pros_and_cons: Natural poise, both in and out of structure. Feet are light, balanced and ready to take off. Willingness to step up in the pocket. Above-average mobility/escapability. Average arm strength for the NFL level. Deep ball accuracy and touch is lacking. Eyes/anticipation must improve.

summary: Ewers is a former five-star quarterback and the No. 1 player in the 2021 recruiting class. He was also the 13th highest-ranked player in 247Sports history. His scouting report—both out of high school and now—starts with his unique arm talent. His high-point, explosive, sidearm release is something rarely seen. It allows him to attempt and complete impressive throws from all platforms. He also displays impressive touch, showcasing his natural playmaking ability when he isn’t overthinking. However, while his release is eye-catching, it is inconsistent. The timing and placement of the ball coming out of his hand are erratic, and his sloppy footwork only exacerbates the issue. He is skittish in the pocket, often muddying clean pockets himself due to poor awareness of when to step up and when to escape. As a result, he appears uncomfortable in clean situations. His accuracy on downfield throws is inconsistent. Despite this, he possesses the arm talent to be a three-level threat as a passer.
pros_and_cons: Has the arm talent to release the ball with zip and accuracy. Explosive, flick-of-the-wrist throwing motion. Has some truly special "feel" or touch throws. Backyard-football-type playmaker. Showed more confidence in 2024. Bad lower-body habits. Inconsistent throwing mechanics lead to inconsistent accuracy. Holds the ball low and loose in his stance.

summary: Gabriel has been on a long college football journey, but the road has led him to an ideal destination. A former three-star recruit and Gatorade High School Football Player of the Year for Hawaii, he traveled about as far from home as possible to play at UCF. After three years there, he transferred to Oklahoma for two seasons before finishing his career at Oregon. A natural left-handed passer, Gabriel is small—below the 10th percentile in both height and weight for the NFL level—but he simply knows how to play the position better than most, reminiscent of Bryce Young in that regard. He throws the most catchable passes in the class. His feet are lightning-quick, allowing him to reset for every throw, and his throwing motion is compact and efficient. He demonstrates a high IQ for the position, navigating the pocket smoothly and confidently while showing the ability to scan the entire field. His overall arm talent is limited and average at best for the NFL. He often has to put his entire body into his throws.
pros_and_cons: Quick movements for fast releases. Quick footwork in the pocket to avoid pressure. Does not panic under pressure. Knows how to get through his progressions, even under duress. Lefty quarterback, which can an adjustment for some receivers. Wide leg kick and open hips compromises accuracy on quick throws. Height will make middle-of-the-field throws a challenge in the NFL. Mobility is adequate for college but won't be as effective in NFL.

summary: Henigan is a former three-star quarterback who was a highly accomplished passer at Billy Ryan High School in Denton, Texas. Over his four-year high school career, he threw for more than 7,000 yards with over 70 passing touchdowns and just 14 interceptions. That starting streak continued at Memphis, where he has been the team's starting quarterback for the past four seasons. He is smaller in stature compared to NFL standards, which contributes to his below-average NFL arm talent. His throwing motion is compact and quick, but he has a tendency to short-arm his follow-through, which negatively impacts his accuracy. Henigan’s footwork on dropbacks is clean, but his lower-body mechanics can become erratic when throwing on the run. He also has a bad habit of retreating in the pocket and throwing off his back foot. His speed won’t be a difference-maker at the next level. That said, he plays with plenty of moxie, which makes him an intriguing player when the ball is in his hands.
pros_and_cons: Displays adequate NFL velocity on short/ intermediate throws. Experienced passer when targeting the middle of the field. Compact and quick throwing motion. Confident, moxie-driven play style. Tends to retreat too far and too often when pressured. Lower-body mechanics can be erratic on follow-throughs. Smaller stature with below-average overall arm talent.

summary: Howard is a former three-star quarterback who excelled in both football and basketball at Downingtown West High School, scoring over 1,000 points on the court. He committed to Kansas State, where he played for four seasons, earning sporadic starts in his first three years before locking down the full-time starting job in 2023. He then transferred to Ohio State, where he had his most effective and productive season, leading the team through the College Football Playoff. He brings adequate size to the pros, ranking above the 75th percentile in both height and weight. He is also a good athlete for his size, making him a viable threat on scrambles and RPOs. While his arm strength isn’t elite, it’s good enough to attack every level of a defense. He is experienced in reading all forms of coverage and is particularly comfortable throwing hole shots against Cover 2. His fundamentals are generally solid, though he has an elongated follow-through with his back leg.
pros_and_cons: Ideal NFL size for the position. Not hesitant to throw on the run and “be an athlete”. Above-average arm strength. Made every throw in the book at some point in 2024. Real experience under center. 35% of passes on third-and-long were short of the sticks. Some inconsistency with his release point, which affects accuracy. Not as experienced or confident throwing over the middle.

summary: Leonard is a former three-star quarterback from Fairhope, Alabama, where he was a two-sport athlete. He received basketball offers from Samford, Missouri State and North Alabama after averaging more than 20 points per game as a senior but ultimately chose football, committing to Duke. He made one start as a true freshman before becoming the full-time starter for the next two seasons, though he missed a significant portion of the 2023 season due to an ankle injury. He transferred to Notre Dame, where he helped propel the team to a College Football Playoff berth and eventually played for a national championship. Leonard is a well-built quarterback whose most alluring trait is his dual-threat ability. He is a battering-ram-style runner who isn’t afraid to take off, absorb hits and do the dirty work to move the chains. However, his passing remains too inconsistent. While he displays good throwing fundamentals, his accuracy and ball placement are issues.
pros_and_cons: Mobility and escapability are pluses to his game. Has some big plays when scrambling. Willing to go through progressions, front and back side. Can put adequate zip on short and intermediate passes. Consistent throwing fundamentals. Accuracy and ball placement are consistent issues. Pocket management is up and down. Velocity is better than distance.

summary: McCord was a high school football legend, winning three straight state championships and earning Pennsylvania Gatorade Player of the Year honors as a senior. He committed to Ohio State— alongside his high school teammate Marvin Harrison Jr.—and sat behind C.J. Stroud for two seasons before taking over as the full-time starter in 2023. After one year as the starter, McCord transferred to Syracuse for his final season. His play style is a mix of Baker Mayfield and Brock Purdy. He has the mindset of a gunslinger but lacks a true gunslinger arm. His feet are quick and light, allowing him to make throws on short notice with a quick release and follow-through, leading to a fast average time to throw over the last two seasons. He is a fiery competitor but remains relatively calm—or at least confident—in the pocket. McCord led the Power Five in big-time throws but ranked just 22nd in big-time throw percentage. Unfortunately, he also led the Power Five in turnover-worthy plays.
pros_and_cons: Light on his feet, constantly bouncing. Ideal throwing mechanics. Great touch passer, including over the middle. Smart football player who knows how to scan the field. Is a fiery competitor but looks calm in the pocket. Baker Mayfield mentality without a Baker Mayfield arm. Too comfortable throwing off his back foot and fading away. Arm strength appears below average to average for the NFL level.

summary: Mertz is a former four-star quarterback who led his team to back- to-back high school state championship appearances, winning the first and falling short in the second. He was named the Gatorade Kansas Football Player of the Year as a senior in 2018 before committing to Wisconsin. After redshirting his first season, he started the next three years before transferring to Florida, where he was the starting quarterback in 2023 and 2024 before tearing his ACL in Week 7. An older, experienced quarterback, Mertz’s decision-making reflects his extensive starting experience. He generally knows where to go with the ball and when to fire. He has ample experience operating under center from his Wisconsin days. Mertz possesses good size and adequate NFL arm strength, along with decent escapability. His experience serves him well under pressure. He reads defenses well pre-snap and does a good job manipulating defenders with his eyes while working through his progressions on time.
pros_and_cons: Fundamentally sound passer with consistent footwork. Strong understanding of pre-snap reads and progression timing. Adequate arm strength for the pro level. Effectively manipulates defenders with his eyes. Significant experience under center at Wisconsin. Accuracy declines when touch is required. His release causes ball placement issues. Struggled with deep-ball efficiency and accuracy in 2024.

summary: Milroe has one of the strongest arms in the class, and if he isn’t in the Tier 1 NFL arm category, he’s not far behind in Tier 2. That track background also makes him a lethal rushing threat. While his physical gifts make him an alluring prospect to invest in, his inconsistencies are why drafting and playing him early could end poorly. He is not consistently accurate. His twitchy throwing motion means that any deviation in his fundamentals can negatively impact ball placement. He also holds onto the ball too long, averaging over 3.00 seconds per dropback, leading to a high sack rate. He also struggles to read non-primary defenders — he can key in on one or two defenders pre-snap but fail to see the full coverage picture post-snap. Though he is a great athlete, his passing grades and efficiency on the run are poor. He does, however, post strong numbers on third-and-long, with more than 50% of his throws going beyond the sticks and a solid number of big-time throws.
pros_and_cons: Not just escapability but a true dual-threat athlete. Good enough athlete to force missed tackles in space. Twitchy athleticism evident in throwing motion speed. Can show really nice touch/accuracy on deep passes. Experienced RPO quarterback. Accuracy/decision-making variance is large right now. Holds the ball low and loose in his stance. Accuracy can dip when he takes speed off his throws. Time to throw/sacks taken is far too high.

summary: Rourke hails from the Great White North of Oakville, Ontario, where he led his team to a Halton Championship as a junior and finished as a runner-up the following season. He spent four years at Ohio as a multi-year starter before transferring to Indiana for his final season of eligibility. As a Hoosier, he had his most productive and efficient year. At over 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Rourke ranks above the 75th percentile in both height and weight. In 2024, he posted a career-low 2.5% turnover-worthy play rate while recording a 5.9% big-time throw rate, the second- highest of his career. His footwork and follow-through are solid, creating an aesthetically clean throwing motion for a passer his size. His accuracy is generally good, though not elite, and he has shown the ability to make impressive touch throws. However, his reliance on touch throws is partly due to a backhanded compliment—he has had plenty of practice with them because his arm strength and velocity are lacking, even for his size.
pros_and_cons: Smooth, fundamentally sound throwing motion. Touch is a plus in his passing game. Has some excellent ball-placement throws. Lacks expected velocity for his size. He is slow-moving outside the pocket. Tends to lock onto reads, struggling to feel and react to pressure.

summary: If you didn’t know his last name, you’d still recognize that Shedeur has NFL bloodlines—or at least that he’s been around high-level football minds—just from watching his tape. He has followed his father as head coach from Jackson State to Colorado and has developed into a legitimate NFL prospect. His scouting report starts with his clean fundamentals. At under the 30th percentile in both height (6-foot-1.5) and weight (215 pounds), those fundamentals are paramount, allowing him to maximize his average arm talent. His throwing motion is highly repeatable, leading to good accuracy and ball placement. His experience at the position helps him see the field well, both pre- and post-snap, resulting in very few turnovers and turnover- worthy plays throughout his career. His mobility is limited, especially by NFL standards. His top trait is likely his mentality— he’s tough as nails in the pocket and has delivered some true “ice in his veins” throws under pressure and on big downs.
pros_and_cons: Strong, wide base with good size in the lower half. Repeatable, fundamentally sound throwing. Good zip on passes within 25 yards. Mental and physical toughness to step up and take a hit. Good feel/anticipation for attacking zone. Ball speed can die on him in the air beyond 40 yards. Release speed is average-to-below-average. Arm strength is average for NFL standards.

summary: Shough is a big-bodied quarterback with ideal NFL size. He has a good but not great arm. He can zip passes into tight windows over the middle and has a higher big-time throw percentage than turnover-worthy play percentage in that area. He is at his best when throwing with velocity but also displays good touch and ball placement on deep passes—though he becomes more inconsistent at shorter distances. One of the older prospects in the class, coming from the 2018 recruiting cycle. He spent three years at Oregon before playing three more at Texas Tech and finishing his career at Louisville. His injury history is concerning, with two season-ending collarbone injuries and a broken fibula on his record. In terms of pocket management, he must be more willing to step up. Too often, he fades away on throws even when pressure is not imminent. While he won’t offer much in terms of mobility or playmaking outside of structure, he has the arm talent to attempt and complete throws from various arm angles.
pros_and_cons: Adequate height to make throws over the middle of the field. NFL-caliber arm talent with the ability to throw with good velocity. Arm strength is good, though not great. Shows the ability to apply the correct touch on passes. Extensive injury history. Limited mobility and escapability by NFL standards. Footwork and ability to align with his target are inconsistent.

summary: Ward's journey from zero-star recruit to potentially the top quarterback in his class is inspiring. His overlooked and underappreciated path shapes his character and gameplay. He believed in himself when most others didn’t, making him one of the most confident quarterbacks in any situation. His arm strength is good for the NFL, though not in the top tier. His throwing style is unorthodox and unique—he consistently throws with a sidearm motion, holds the ball low and often misaligns his hips and feet when throwing. As a result, his ball placement can be erratic, though it has also produced some incredible throws. His reads and progressions are generally correct, but he too often locks onto the biggest or longest throw. Despite the chaotic nature of his play style, he has graded highly in almost every stable category — an ironic truth, given the visual instability of his quarterback play.
pros_and_cons: True sidearm release that is David Carr-esque. Experienced and successful middle-of-field passer. Never say die type of playmaker with good escapability. Adequate arm strength for the NFL level. Impressive and natural touch passer. Holds the ball below the shoulders, making for a longer release. Side arm release is exotic but feels too varied throw-to-throw. Accuracy numbers are high, but ball placement isn't consistent.

summary: McLaughlin played over 1,800 snaps as Alabama before transferring to Ohio State and winning the Rimington Award as the nation's best center. Though his grading profile was closer to above average than elite, McLaughlin allowed just 1 sack and 8 quarterback hits in his career. His extensive big game experience is an asset, though he missed the Buckeyes' playoff run due to a torn Achilles suffered in November.
pros_and_cons: Good sense of where he needs to be at all times. Functional enough athlete to fit in most schemes. Works hard to create proper angles in run game. Torn achilles puts 2025 status in doubt. Struggles with snaps that included tinkering with mechanics. Has a hard time staying in front of defenders with quicker first step.

summary: Monheim is a highly athletic player who played four of the five offensive line positions at USC. He put together two solid seasons at tackle before moving inside to center in 2024, where he did not allow a sack and earned the second-highest PFF run- blocking grade of his career. Despite a couple of tough performances against top defenses like Michigan and Notre Dame, Monheim showed that he has a chance to function in an NFL offense with his combination of quickness and football IQ if he can get stronger and play in the right system.
pros_and_cons: Plus athlete with experience at 4 of 5 offensive line positions. Very light on his feet. Moves laterally with ease. Plenty capable of getting out on screens or long pulls. Quickness and high IQ allow him to make adjustments on the fly. Moved inside from tackle due to very short arms. Lack of length causes him to reach at defenders. Below-average lower-body strength.

summary: Slater earned 44 starts in his four-year college career, capping it off as an FCS All-American in 2024. He has an ideal interior offensive lineman build with good total weight and weight distribution. He is light on his feet despite his bigger size. That helps him get his whole body into recovery/reaction mode when pass-rushers hit their moves, especially across his face. He has a wide, low base in his pre-snap stance, which creates consistent leverage when firing off the ball. He has some reps where he dips his eyes or gets a bit too far on his toes and allows quicker pass- rushers to cross his face or attack a shoulder more easily. He has good but not elite grip strength, which can get him in trouble when his hands shoot too narrowly and defensive linemen can disengage quickly. Though he is at a good weight, it can look like he lacks some density to be a boulder to move in the middle. He will need to lean into his quickness as a difference-making trait.
pros_and_cons: Ideal interior offensive lineman build. Long arms for a center. Light on his feet in pass protection and when climbing or pulling. Natural athlete who just happens to play offensive line. Wide, low base pre-snap. Lack a powerful punch at contact. Hand placement can be too narrow. Can dip his eyes and get crossed up by quicker interior rushers.

summary: Wilson ranked in the 97th percentile in PFF’s Game Athleticism Score metric in each of the past two seasons. His movement skills are a plus in many areas. Beyond just being able to get out on the hoof for mid and outside zone, his explosive first step allows him to dictate contact for pin-and-pull power concepts and slide protections. His hands are generally well placed and fast enough to get inside consistently. Wilson does seem to lack some length, causing him to be a bit on his toes and leaning if asked to reach for contact. He doesn't have imposing strength but does mitigate that well with good anchoring technique and flexibility. He shows some inexperience with a lack of anticipation when guessing wrong one-on-one with defensive tackles.
pros_and_cons: Excellent movement skills. Flexible hips and hamstrings to get low in his stance. Coordinated footwork for long shuffles when mirroring. Quick hands to get up and inside of defenders after the snap. Good anchoring technique to counter bull rushes. Doesn't possess imposing strength. Inexperience shows in lack of anticipation w/pass-rush set-ups.

summary: Zabel started his career as a reserve lineman at North Dakota State before becoming a full-time starter in 2022. He earned FCS All-American honors in his final season. He is a well-built prospect who wins in very translatable ways. His lack of length will likely kick him inside, but he could play tackle in a pinch. Zabel’s feet are light and can mirror pass-rushers well. He has excellent grip strength to latch on and maintain blocks. His plus core strength helps there, too. His leg drive is consistent and effective, though he will likely be a better zone blocker than a man/gap scheme blocker due to NFL-level strength and size. His power at punch can be average, and his hands can shoot high. His patience in pass blocking is a big plus, as is his hip/hamstring flexibility to stay low in his stance despite his 6-foot-6 frame. He brings great balance to recover against unexpected power. At the Senior Bowl, he was lights-out at guard and center.
pros_and_cons: Top-tier grip strength. Very good at lining up tackles between the shoulders. Great athlete. Explosive first step to thrive in a zone blocking scheme. Leg drive is constant and effective. Length will likely kick him inside. 90th-percentile height/weight. Smaller hands and shorter arms. Hands can slide up and off target against more powerful players.

summary: At 6-foot-5 and near 330 pounds, he checks all the size boxes. He has excellent pre-snap posture thanks to his long arms — he can touch the ground while keeping his back flat. He has very high football intelligence. His weight is well distributed with minimal bad weight and good mass/power in the lower half. He could use a bit more force at contact on a consistent basis, but it is nothing glaring, and he even has some snaps where he can really move defenders against their will. His functional athleticism is adequate — he can get on the hoof as a puller and not look unnatural. If there is a potential glaring issue, it likely comes from his foot speed. When he is braced and ready, he can have a strong base, but when caught off guard, he doesn't have elite core strength and can get knocked off balance more easily than expected. He is praised for his competitiveness, leadership, high football IQ and work ethic.
pros_and_cons: Well-built guard with NFL size. Strong hands and core to not disengage after moves. Very long arms for an interior player. High IQ lineman. Finisher's mentality. Balance can be off at times. Below average foot speed. Can get caught behind when defender cross his face.

summary: Colby is a rugged zone blocking guard who twice earned All-Big Ten team selections, including a First-Team selection in 2024. Listed at 6-foot-6 and 310 pounds, Colby has an ideal build and a mean streak that presents itself well in the run game. He turned in his best season in 2024 as a run blocker under Tim Lester, who shifted the Hawkeyes' offense to more of an outside zone-based scheme. Colby's flaws lie in his consistent struggles in pass protection regardless of position. He likely is a depth piece in an outside zone offense because his pass-blocking needs major development before he can be considered a starting-caliber player.
pros_and_cons: Mean streak in the run game. Found comfort on outside zone runs in 2024. Nice drive in his lower half when he engages defenders downhill. Consistent problems in true pass sets. Struggles with length despite being listed at 6-foot-6. Tendency to lunge toward pass-rushers instead of staying patient.

summary: Cooper is a functional zone-blocking guard who spent six years in college, earning a starting spot in the last two. As a five-time All-Big Ten Academic Team selection, he makes up for mediocre athleticism and below-average strength by understanding where he needs to be at all times while creating proper angles at the point of attack. Cooper is likely to fit in an outside zone scheme, where his positive traits in the run game can shine while he continues to get stronger. His experience at both guard spots gives him at least some versatility, assuming he starts his NFL career as a backup.
pros_and_cons: Understands where he needs to be in the run game/pass pro. Above average technique and movement skills. Moves feet well to create proper angles. Experience at both guard spots. Lack of strength shows when run-blocking / dealing with bull rushes. Shorter arms create problems dealing with lengthier DTs. Average athleticism doesn’t make up for below-average power.

summary: Dellinger is a sturdy guard who has posted consistently positive pass blocking production after arriving at LSU as a four-star prospect. He boasts enough strength to handle stronger defensive tackles by himself in pass protection and gives a nice initial punch in the run game. His 2024 season was unfortunately cut short due to injury, but returned in time to perform reasonably well at the Senior Bowl, even taking some reps at center in the process.
pros_and_cons: Good initial punch in the run game. Functional strength that can match up well with stronger DTs. Experience at four different OL positions. Below average length leads to lunging and balance issues. Tendency to sell out for big blocks. Mediocre lateral movement.

summary: Fairchild is a two-year starter at left guard for Georgia who posted a nearly elite 89.2 pass blocking grade across the past two seasons. While he isn't quite as powerful as his teammate Tate Ratledge, he is equally adept with his footwork in pass protection and is athletic enough to function as a puller or at the second level. Fairchild has a reasonably high floor as a candidate to serve as interior depth for a team in need of functional pass protectors. If he can get stronger over the next couple of years, he could develop into something more.
pros_and_cons: Well-taught interior pass protector. Keeps feet moving to maintain leverage and angles in run game. Quick out of his stance in pass protection. Doesn't have a singular trait that would be considered dominant. Middling upper body strength doesn’t let him displace defenders. Tendency to lean into run blocks with shoulders/chest.

summary: Frazier started his career as a left tackle at FIU, earning one of the higher grades in Conference USA at his position as a redshirt freshman in 2021. He then transferred to LSU and kicked inside where his athleticism made him a plus pass protector. That ability allowed him to not allow a sack in the final 20 games of his career, including his final game against Baylor in which he started at right tackle. Frazier's athleticism and versatility give him a chance to at least stick in the NFL as a swingman.
pros_and_cons: Former tackle with above average athleticism inside. Doesn't panic when presented with stunts up front. Solid footwork and balance in pass sets. Average length is a problem when defenders get into his pads. Some struggles to adjust when defenders cross his face. Occasionally caught lunging due to length issues.

summary: Gray was a four-year starter at left tackle for Oregon State and was one of the few players to stay in Corvallis after head coach Jonathan Smith’s departure heading into 2024. He moved inside to left guard for his final season, improving his overall grade from 2023, albeit against weaker competition. He's a functional zone blocker who adjusted reasonably well to a greater variety of schemes this past season. Gray’s biggest question is whether he can effectively pass protect at the next level after posting sub- 65.0 pass-blocking grades in each of his five seasons as a starter.
pros_and_cons: Versatility that could help him stick on a roster. Functional outside zone blocker. Climbs to the second level with urgency. Makes a point to finish linebackers once he seals them off. Not long/nimble enough for OT. Not strong enough for OG. Consistently below-average pass protector regardless of position. Shorter arms and lack of strength are an issue against bigger DTs.

summary: Jackson was the top interior offensive line recruit in the nation in 2021 and certainly didn't disappoint during his time in Columbus. He earned three First-Team All-Big Ten selections, including in 2024 when he moved to left tackle during the team's final nine games and performed admirably. Jackson has a high floor with an ideal guard build and enough consistency to project as an NFL starter. While he isn't always the most dominant player on the field, his combination of footwork and technique could help just about any team looking for a starting-caliber guard.
pros_and_cons: Sound footwork in all phases. Works hard to gain proper positioning in zone run game. Rarely overpowered in pass protection. Moved to LT over final nine games and performed well. More consistently stable than dominant style of play. Can get caught off guard by stunts. Needs to work on pace and leverage when getting to second level.

summary: Jones was a top-100 recruit in the 2022 high school class and the No. 6 interior offensive lineman overall. Despite his listed position coming out of high school, he started for the Tigers at right tackle immediately as a true freshman and has been there for his entire three-year career. However, it seems like the recruiting services nailed Jones' projection because he'd likely be best at guard in the NFL. That's because he has heavy footwork in pass protection, which makes him susceptible to being beaten around the edge. He's a powerful player with excellent length, though, and those traits should still shine at guard.
pros_and_cons: Long arms, especially for a guard - 92nd percentile. Big, heavy hands that shock on impact. Good anchor in pass protection. Three years of starting experience in the SEC. Heavy feet at tackle can expose him against speed rushers. Inconsistent hand placement lets defenders to get into his chest. Plays on his toes too much in the run game.

summary: Kandra is a former three-star prospect who played on both sides of the ball in high school prior to committing to Louisville. He followed head coach Scott Satterfield to Cincinnati, where he became one of the more effective all-around guards in the country over the past two seasons. Standing at 6-foot-4, Kandra is a high-cut athlete who wins with plus athleticism and consistent technique. His lack of bend and shorter arms are a cause for concern regarding his ceiling, but there is enough to work with to think he could be developed into a starter in due time.
pros_and_cons: Measured approach in the run game, gaining proper leverage. Much improved in pass protection in 2024, particularly 1v1. Few consistently poor habits with regard to technique. High pad level leads to bending at the waist. Most of his pressures in 2024 involved him as the target on stunts. Rarely a powerful force, which could limit him to outside zone.

summary: Lampkin is a fascinating case of a player testing the limits of how small a player can be on the offensive line. Standing at just 5-foot- 10 and 270 pounds, Lampkin put together a dominant five-year career spread across Coastal Carolina and North Carolina. He overcomes his diminutive stature with top-tier competitive spirit and excellent technique, particularly in the zone running game, where he's earned an elite 90.6 run-blocking grade over the past two seasons. Lampkin also shined as the last player added to the Senior Bowl roster, showing off his skills and determination against some of the nation's best defensive tackles.
pros_and_cons: Five years of excellent production across two schools. High level of competitive spirit, consistently plays to the whistle. Excellent footwork on zone runs. Understands that he has a leverage advantage due to his height. Significant experience at all three interior positions. Lack of height can leave him overwhelmed vs powerful bull rushes. Lack of length is an issue when defenders hold his shoulder pads. Doesn't cover a ton of ground with his first step.

summary: On 1,155 pass blocking snaps at left tackle over that three year period, he did not allow a single sack. His best reps come when run blocking. He shows good tenacity with a strong punch at contact before following it up with great grip strength to latch on and take defenders for a ride. He has the initial explosiveness to block inside and mid-zone concepts but is most impactful when blocking power. Though he is listed at 6-foot-6, his arm length is well below average for offensive tackle play in the league. This causes him to lean into contact at times, often becoming unbalanced and too on his toes. Where he has good first-step quickness, some stiffness in his lower half movements make shuffling with a defender across his face and deep dropbacks in pass protection a challenge. He is also upright in his stance, which can cause some balance issues when asked to pivot and anchor. When he can keep defenders square between the shoulders, he has good anchoring technique and strength.
pros_and_cons: Good balance when taking contact. Really strong grip strength. Sound, consistent anchoring technique. Reliable run blocking in both man and zone. Smart, aware player. First step is slower; struggles to catch up against speed rushers. Too much on his toes; leaning into contact gets him in trouble. Appears to have some stiffness in his hips.

summary: Ratledge has been a three year-starter at right guard for Georgia, including their national championship run during the 2022 season. He dealt with injury in 2024, but allowed just 7 pressures and 1 sack across just over 300 opportunities. He has been consistently one of the best interior pass protectors in the nation throughout his career while steadily improving in the run game. While he isn't the fleetest of foot, Ratledge's solid technique gives him a chance to be a starter at the next level.
pros_and_cons: Initial punch plays up on first level in duo/inside zone schemes. Consistently sound pass sets. Light on his feet and quick with his hands early in pass reps. Average athleticism. Tendency to lose angles in run game. Susceptible to counter moves in run game after initial punch.

summary: Rivers is a former four-star prospect who battled through injuries during his time at Miami. He was an All-ACC selection in his lone healthy season in 2023, which was also his only season solely playing left tackle. He followed that up in 2024 with a career-high 78.8 pass-blocking grade while oscillating between left guard and left tackle within games during the second half of the season. That versatility could serve him well in the NFL, but middling athleticism and foot speed likely make him a better option as a guard.
pros_and_cons: Guard/tackle versatility. Keeps legs driving downhill in the run game. Proper hand setup in pass protection, particularly at tackle. Tries to strike first. Middling athleticism causes problems against quicker rushers. Slower feet limit him to down blocks and short pulls in run game. Slightly high pad level doesn’t let him readjust feet sometimes.

summary: Webb is a former five-star recruit and state champion wrestler who played his first two seasons at Georgia before transferring to Jacksonville State and starting at left guard for three years. He immediately became the Gamecocks' best offensive lineman and earned First-Team All-Conference USA selections in 2023 and 2024. Webb appears to be a bit on the smaller side, though weighing in at 310 pounds at the Senior Bowl helps his cause. He makes up for that size with solid athleticism and a willingness to finish his blocks.
pros_and_cons: Grinder who keeps his feet moving and aims to finish blocks. Quick enough to play in any scheme but likely a better fit in zone. Some production as a puller. Mirrors feet well in pass protection. Very few true pass-blocking reps in Jacksonville State's scheme. Lack of length is an issue when engaging in pass protection. Inconsistent hand placement.

summary: Wehr is a former defensive lineman who spent two years as Montana State's right tackle before moving inside to right guard in 2024. He earned a top-10 grade among all FCS offensive linemen in each of his three seasons as a starter, as he used his powerful initial punch and lower body to maul defensive linemen in the run game. He also excelled as a pass protector at the FCS level, allowing just eight pressures and zero sacks in his three seasons on offense. Wehr's ceiling is likely capped by his lack of arm length and lateral quickness, but he could get a chance to stick as a developmental gap scheme guard.
pros_and_cons: Nice punch in downhill run schemes. Strong enough to anchor against bull rushes. Aggressiveness as a former defensive linemen shows often. Doesn't win with much aside from strength advantage. Short arms that are susceptible to counter moves. Below-average lateral quickness limits his scheme flexibility.

summary: Banks, a five-star recruit, started at left tackle for Texas since his true freshman season. He is on the smaller side (6-foot-5) for an NFL tackle. His arm length isn't a strength, evident in how he leans into contact and onto his heels at times. Long defensive linemen can easily get their hands inside and pull him to the side on push-pull moves. There is otherwise a lot to love. Banks is a great athlete, especially for a 320-pounder. He carries a good amount of weight in his lower half and posterior chain to create power and anchor against bull rushes. He is excellent on the hoof in mid- and outside-zone blocking schemes (though his feet can get clumsy). As a pulling blocker, he is a heat-seeking missile at the second level. Banks has the balance and foot speed to mirror pass-rushers and hit appropriate depth, but he needs to work on his grip strength to maintain blocks longer. His run-blocking ability and length could push him inside to guard.
pros_and_cons: Flexible hips and wide base for powerful stance. Foot speed/explosiveness is top tier. Great second-level/space blocker. Natural athleticism gives him high zone-blocking potential. Really impressive balance for 320-plus-pound player. Height hints at shorter arm length, which shows on tape. Too susceptible to push-pull moves. Needs to improve grip strength to latch on and hold blocks.

summary: A zero-star recruit from the 2019 class, Belton spent his first few seasons at the JUCO level before transferring to NC State. After sitting for one year behind a top-10 pick in Ikem Ekwonu, he took over for him at left tackle in 2022 and held that spot for the following three seasons. Like Ekwonu, Belton has the length and strength to overpower defenders. He's also more explosive than most 350-pound tackles, as he can fire off the ball to find defenders at the second level or seal them off at the line of scrimmage. His raw power also gives him a good anchor in pass protection against bull rushes. Belton is still raw in a number of areas, including his punch timing, pad level and footwork. While he's an explosive athlete, he's not very quick. He has had issues with speed rushers in the past. Even though a sixth-year prospect with as many technical issues as Belton has could put off some teams, he has the tools to become a starting-caliber tackle down the line.
pros_and_cons: Good length and raw power at 345 pounds. More explosive than expected. Gets to second level with ease. Stonewalls power rushers with strength in pass protection. Lacks high-end lateral quickness. Late hands in pass protection, letting defenders into his chest. Footwork needs work. Causes him to be off-balance at times.

summary: Campbell is a former four-star recruit who started every game he played in (38) across three years at LSU. Campbell isn't shy about communicating pre-snap. He makes calls and adjustments, and he'll even look back to tell the running back where the extra pressure is coming from. That football IQ gives him a high floor projection at tackle, guard or even center. His footwork, balance and posture are all fantastic. His hands are quick, precise and patient to frustrate rushers. He has good technique to handle power in pass protection but doesn't dish out punishment in the run game as well. He is listed at 6-foot-6, but his arm length doesn't match. You can tell his length is below ideal NFL thresholds. That shows up against longer, quicker edge players — and could be a reason why NFL teams don't see him as a starting offensive tackle. He also has a narrower, higher pad level base. If you can live with some of those deficiencies, there is so much to love.
pros_and_cons: Narrow base, but generally strong and balanced. Body movements are quick, compact and precise. Hands are up and active, always ready to strike with power. Great grip and core strength to maintain blocks. Foot speed is quick enough and well balanced, but not top tier. Higher pre-snap stance leads to high pad level when engaging. Shorter arm length. Lack of flexibility in groin to stretch kicks/protect outside shoulder.

summary: Conerly was the highest-rated offensive lineman to ever commit to Oregon, so it’s no surprise that he played more than 100 snaps as a true freshman before earning a starting job for 2023 and 2024. His movement skills and length are starting-caliber for the NFL, and his pre-snap stance is wide and athletic, leaving him ready to explode up or back. His foot speed allows him to run gracefully in zone blocking and mirror pass-rushers. His hands are quick to strike and reset but inconsistent in placement and patience. He can be a strong player but doesn't always show it. When he confidently lines up defenders between the shoulders, he packs a good punch. When caught off guard, he is too easily discarded. The 21-year-old lacks consistent displacement strength for power blocking schemes. He is a competitive player who shows good effort through the whistle. Ideally, he won't have to start right away in the NFL, giving him time to improve and unlock a high talent ceiling.
pros_and_cons: Quick, explosive offensive tackle. Quick footwork to keep his weight under him while mirroring. Good on the hoof in a zone blocking scheme. Quick hands for hand fighting/resetting. Shows competitive toughness and fight through reps. Inconsistent hand placement/striking location. Lower weight profile does limit displacement strength in run game. Must continue to get functionally stronger.

summary: Cornelius was once a zero-star offensive guard recruit before manning the right side of Oregon's offensive line after transferring to the team in 2023. He is a big-bodied player who is listed below the 50th percentile in height and weight but doesn't play like it. His arms appear to be longer and much closer to average for the NFL, and he carries a good amount of his weight in his middle and upper body, as well as in his glutes, to give him a more hulking appearance and play style. Cornelius’ feet can look heavy, and his first step isn't overly impressive. But he does have long strides to not be a liability in space when run blocking. He has long arms but needs to be more consistent in maximizing them. There are plenty of reps where he engages and pushes defenders off him but then allows them to get right back into his chest instead of latching on to maintain blocks.
pros_and_cons: Covers a lot of ground despite not being explosive or quick. Arm length appears to be well above average for the NFL. Adequate lower-body strength for anchor and leg drive. Good anchoring technique versus bull rushes. Good combo blocker. Not overly quick in his first movements. Does not play with his arm fully extended enough. Can get beat on the outside shoulder versus top speed rushers.

summary: Crenshaw-Dickson played a lot of college football. Across five years at San Diego State and one year at Florida, he logged more than 3,000 snaps. He has a massive frame at 6-foot-7 and 315 pounds with long arms. But beyond just being able to match the long arms of defensive linemen, he knows his length allows him to be patient and wait for pass-rushers to show their hands before countering. The 24-year-old is a smart, patient blocker who possesses good anticipation and pre-snap recognition for pass- rush plans. His somewhat leaner frame gives him decent mobility, and his weight distribution gives him good balance. He seems to lack some strength. He's a decent athlete but doesn't have the speed-to-power explosiveness to truly move people in the run game. Crenshaw-Dickson’s intelligence for angles and landmarks makes him more effective as a zone blocker. He doesn't make many mistakes, and most of his bad plays stem from facing quicker or stronger players.
pros_and_cons: Tall offensive tackle with good arm length. Somewhat slender build gives him athletic movement skills. Constantly communicating pre-snap to call out potential blitzers. Highly intelligent player with good patience and anticipation. Coordinated at lining up defenders in space. Lacks the weight/density to slow down power quickly. Doesn't show imposing strength in man/gap run blocking. Can struggle to reposition his hands vs. speed moves.

summary: Ersery was a three-year starter at left tackle for Minnesota from 2022-2024. His size stands out, as he measures 6-foot-6 and 330 pounds. He is light on his feet despite his size and has an explosive first step that yielded high PFF run-blocking grades in zone assignments. Ersery has the foot quickness to make it to his landmarks in pass protection but can struggle against fast edge rushers, sometimes because he’s high-waisted. His pad level is high pre-snap and he pops up high when the ball is snapped, which allows bendier edge rushers to get under his arm. To mitigate that, he lunges — which gets his weight too far on his toes and off balance. When Ersery keeps rushers between the shoulders, he has the girth and weight to anchor, neutralize and move them. He has good eyes on stunts and twists but can struggle to stay in front of rushers when they get across his face one-on-one.
pros_and_cons: Adequate size and length for the NFL. Light on his feet for a player of his size. Explosive first step and top speed for 330 pounds. Impressive pass-blocking hand work. Good footwork when anchoring. High-waisted player. Weight is too on his toes right now. Can struggle to mirror versus cross-face moves.

summary: Grant is a late bloomer who didn't step on a football field until his junior year of high school. His background as an all-state high school wrestler gives him an edge up front that he often uses to his advantage. Grant is quick and powerful on his feet with the ability to get to any spot in the run game. He also sets up and anchors well when presented with an opposing bull rush. While he could play a bit more in control in space and needs to refine his hand technique in pass protection, the true question for Grant is how he will adjust to NFL competition after spending all five of his collegiate seasons at the FCS level.
pros_and_cons: Light and powerful in lower body. Above-average lateral quickness. Gets across defenders on reach blocks with ease. Advances to second level quickly. Wrestling background gives him a finisher's mentality. Will face a serious jump in competition. Low hand setup in pass protection allows defenders into his chest. Struggles to gear his feet down when sizing up defenders.

summary: Lundt was a two-star recruit after playing just two years of high school football. He committed to UConn, and after redshirting the 2019 season and losing the 2020 season to the pandemic, he started at right tackle for four straight seasons. Lundt’s calling card is his length (around 6-foot-7). His long arms allow him to keep distance between himself and defenders to mitigate long- arm moves. They also help him dictate contact. His footwork (coordination and speed) improved over his college career, and he is decently balanced for his taller frame. He is listed below 290 pounds, which would rank in the last percentile for the NFL, but his weight is distributed evenly. Lundt’s best run-game work comes in zone blocking concepts, as his movements and length allow him to angle defenders. He struggles to get push when blocking power concepts. He also lacks the necessary sand in the pants to anchor, especially when defenders get a leverage advantage on him.
pros_and_cons: Elite length thanks to 6-foot-8 frame. Good eyes when climbing to the second level. Decent foot speed for a player of his size. Only four penalties across 1,700 snaps in two years. Nearly 0-percentile weight right now. Lacks the strength to get in the way of defenders. Hands can be erratic before the punch in pass protection.

summary: Mbow started at guard and tackle for Purdue, and he played right tackle in 2024. He's only 300 pounds — and looks like he could be even slimmer. He has a fast play style with an explosive first step and quick footwork. He can reach any depth in pass blocking and easily mirrors cross-face moves. He dictates contact by getting his hands on defenders first. Mbow absorbs contact and stays balanced with excellent core strength and an ability to redirect. He creates a pop at contact but struggles with strength overall. He is too easy to stack and shed for NFL-caliber linemen. He also struggles to anchor at times. He is more impactful as a zone blocker than a man/gap blocker. His hands are fast, but they can be wide and misplaced, creating more of a hug than a block (which can cause holding penalties). Mbow’s competitiveness will never be in question. He could be a starter at all five line positions, although he must improve his pad level to play center.
pros_and_cons: Fleet of foot, getting out in space as a puller or in zone blocking. Quick, well-coordinated footwork in pass protection. Relentless leg drive when run blocking. Adequate arm length for tackle position in NFL. Always generates a "pop" at contact. Lighter weight makes run blocking/displacing more challenging. Wide hands to hug defenders too often. Naturally high in his pre-snap stance.

summary: Membou was a multi-sport athlete in high school, participating in football, wrestling and tennis. He committed to Missouri and started for the Tigers over the past three years. He has excellent natural flexibility, foot coordination and balance. That allows him to move well when blocking for zone concepts and when taking on contact. He also has an explosive first step for combo blocks. He is listed at 325 pounds but could use more consistency in his power. He may give up a good amount of ground against NFL- level bull rushes and needs to really lean and engage his leg drive to displace between the tackles. He was much improved in how controlled he played from 2023 to 2024, which makes him someone you want to buy into as just a true junior heading to the NFL. He is very impressive in jump, 45-degree and vertical sets in pass protection.
pros_and_cons: Good hip/hamstring flexibility to sit in his stance. Low and explosive out of his stance. Naturally coordinated in his movements and footwork. Feet can move quickly. Looks great on the hoof as a puller and lead blocker. Can struggle to anchor on the edge despite being 325 pounds. Needs more strength for maintaining blocks. Could use more of a finisher's mentality.

summary: Nelson is an experienced offensive tackle prospect who started at guard and tackle for Wisconsin over the past four years. He sizes up well at just over 6-foot-6, but his weight (around 310 pounds) is lower for NFL standards. However, his lower weight does align with his play strengths. Nelson has quick footwork and a nice first step to be an effective zone run blocker. He shows good technique and timing to wall off defenders and create rushing lanes. He mirrors decently well in pass protection. When he gets his hands inside to latch on, he has good grip strength, footwork and balance to maintain blocks. However, his pad level is naturally high and he lacks some sand in his pants, which causes him to get off balance. Although he is without displacement power and doesn't consistently make an impact in man/gap run-blocking concepts, he can be an effective combo blocker. His hands are often too low before he makes contact, exposing his chest.
pros_and_cons: Long frame with good length for the NFL. Quick footwork out of his stance. Good grip strength to maintain blocks. Good anchoring technique to get under and elevate. High pad level pre- and post-snap. Shows some stiffness/inflexibility to really get his butt down. Looks off balance when retreating in kick slides.

summary: Pierce is a former walk-on who became Rutgers' first offensive lineman to earn All-Big Ten honors. He carries a massive 6-foot-8 frame that he has worked to slim down to less than 350 pounds over the past four years. All that work paid off in a big way in 2024, as he ranked among the 12 highest-graded tackles in the FBS. Pierce's height and length jump off the tape, and his lateral quickness has improved as he has slimmed down his frame. He still needs some work and will continue to battle with a lack of bend, but his potential at this size is certainly something to dream about.
pros_and_cons: Ridiculous frame. 6-foot-8 and 345 pounds. Can overwhelm smaller defenders with height and length. Slightly better lateral quickness in 2024 than in previous years. Good initial hand usage in pass protection. Lower half isn't as strong as frame suggests. Struggles to bend and can get caught lunging in pass protection. Difficulties stopping and readjusting his feet.

summary: Savaiinaea was a three-year college starter with significant experience at three different positions across the line. He made PFF's All-Freshman team while playing right guard in 2022 before moving to tackle over the past two seasons. Savaiinaea has long been a competent pass protector whose footwork and hand usage are among his greatest assets. His ability to stay light on his feet allows him to deter outside speed rushes, though he could be better at reacting back to counter inside moves. The real issue in his game is a lack of strength, particularly in the run game, where he will likely fit better in a zone scheme. At the very least, an NFL team is getting a reliable swingman with the potential to turn into a starter if he can develop in the weight room.
pros_and_cons: Substantial experience at tackle and guard. Competent pass protector, regardless of position. Active feet in pass protection. Rarely caught on his heels. Engages hands quickly to deter outside rush. Lack of strength shows in consistently below-average run blocking. Trouble adjusting back to inside moves. Issues dealing with length due to lack of upper-body strength.

summary: Simmons was a three-star interior offensive lineman recruit before committing to San Diego State. He redshirted his first year with the Aztecs and started every game at right tackle the following season. He then transferred to Ohio State, where he flipped to the left side. Simmons was having his best year yet before tearing his ACL five games into the 2024 season. Before his injury, he displayed high-level NFL traits. He isn't the biggest or longest tackle, but he makes up for it with elite flexibility. He can get very low pre-snap and impressively maintains that pad level while moving in a loaded and squatted position to maximize power at punch and neutralize bull rushes. The 22-year-old has quick, precise hands, always looking to get inside leverage. His footwork is balanced, and his core strength is excellent for maintaining blocks while twisting and turning. He lacks some strength to displace defenders in the run game, but he has enough to counter rushes.
pros_and_cons: Fantastic balance and can slide and mirror while squatted. Consistently low pad level at contact. Adequate length for the NFL. Footwork is quick and slide length is adequate. Competitive, consistently plays through the whistle. Hands have a low starting point. No true displacement strength in the run game. Lower weight makes anchoring tougher.

summary: Trapilo was a four-star recruit, and his father, Steve, was an All- American offensive lineman at Boston College and played in the NFL. Trapilo opted to continue the Boston College lineage, becoming a full-time starter in 2022. Trapilo, after playing left tackle in his first year as a starter, featured at right tackle for the past two seasons. He has ideal length and size at 6-foot-7 and 310 pounds. He is patient with good eyes for where and how pressure might arise before the ball is snapped. He is a bit lighter on the scale for an offensive tackle but doesn't play like it. He has a strong first step and a strong punch at contact with good leg drive for combo blocking. He consistently tries to maximize his length advantage in pass protection. He has a bit of an imbalance because of his height, and there are a handful of reps each game where he is slower than he needs to be when trying to mirror stunts and twists.
pros_and_cons: Ideal height and length for the NFL. Strong initial first step to get his body going where it needs. Eyes always searching for something to block. Patient hands in pass protection. Good leg drive to displace on combo blocks. Plays with his head down too much. Needs to keep his eyes up. Height comes with some natural imbalance. Slow to turn to face stunts and twists.

summary: Williams is built like an NFL offensive tackle, checking all the boxes for height, weight and length. He is a younger player with only one year of starting experience at Texas. His game is more about flashes than consistency, but the flashes are why we're talking about him. Williams’ arm length allows him to keep pass- rushers at bay — at least when he gets his hands up quickly enough. He has good power when making contact but must do a better job of keeping defenders between his shoulders to showcase that. His pass-blocking reps lack anticipation, as does most of his game. His hands are often off, both in their placement (usually very wide) and timing (late). Once he locks on, he can take defenders for a ride. Although he can explode well off the first step, his feet can appear heavy. He was also called for 13 penalties in 2024 (seven false starts and five holding).
pros_and_cons: Excellent size for an offensive tackle. Ideal arm length that looks longer than height suggests. First-step explosiveness is noteworthy for his weight. Strong grip once he locks on. Finisher's mentality. Only a one-year starter. Can explode well for his size, but feet are heavy. Punch timing and placement are inconsistent.

summary: Alexander was a two-star recruit and received only two Division I offers, one of which was Toledo. He redshirted his first year and was a rotational lineman for the next four seasons before earning a full-time starting spot in 2023 and 2024. He brings ideal size at just under 6-foot-4 and 305 pounds with 34-inch arms. That build gives him the potential to play at 3-technique or 3-4 defensive end in the NFL for odd or even fronts. Alexander is strong as an ox, resulting in elite PFF run-defense grades. He has a violent club move that he pairs with a rip or an arm-over to get into the backfield (14.0% pass-rush win rate). He can hold up well against double teams and forklift blockers onto their heels and into the pocket. He could clean up some technical things, such as snap anticipation and maintaining leverage longer out of his stance. He also looks too top-heavy at times. He was one of the Senior Bowl’s standouts, showing a nice twitch as a pass-rusher.
pros_and_cons: Explosive first step gives him a quick speed-to-power transition. Powerful leg drive even when OL are in anchor. Good power in his initial punch to knock OL back on their heels. Violent club move when crossing the face of OL. Strong as an ox in run defense, even against doubles. Tends to pop up quickly and rush high. Can be the last one out of his stance. Weight can be a little too top-heavy and cause imbalance.

summary: Biggers is a former three-star defensive line recruit from Mount Ulla, NC, where he was a three-sport athlete in football, basketball and track at West Rowan High School. He committed to Georgia Tech and saw the field immediately, playing in nine games as a true freshman. He became a full-time starter in 2023 and remained in that role through 2024. At 6-foot-5 and 320 pounds with 35-inch arms, Biggers' sheer size and length stand out before the first snap on tape. His frame challenges interior offensive linemen, particularly shorter-armed centers and guards, especially when he fires off the ball with a solid first step. His length gives him unique advantages in leverage battles, but he struggles to maximize his natural power due to his high pad level. His pass-rush production has been minimal, with a low win percentage over the last two seasons. However, he has a good sense of where the ball is going and plays with solid effort for a player of his size.
pros_and_cons: Massive frame that is difficult to move off the line. Exceptional arm length for an interior lineman, particularly at NT. Strong instincts and awareness to track the ball’s direction. Uses long arms to disrupt passing lanes and bat down throws. Reliable motor and effort level, especially for a player of his size. Struggles to keep pad level low at the snap, giving OL leverage. Despite his length, he misses too many wrap-up tackles. Lacks explosive first step to effectively convert speed to power.

summary: Caldwell was a zero-star offensive line recruit and tried to play offensive line at Hutchinson Community College, but their 2020 season was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. He later walked on at Independence Community College as a defensive lineman, playing one season there before transferring to Sam Houston State for two seasons and then making a big impact as a nose tackle at Oregon in 2024. He brings adequate girth for nose tackle duties at 330-plus pounds. He also has surprisingly quick feet and decent pursuit speed for a player carrying that much weight. He can hold up in double-team situations, which gives him some versatility to play all interior spots in an odd front. He tends to play on the ground/on his knees a bit too much. His short arms also impact how quickly he can disengage blocks and how well he can wrap up ball carriers.
pros_and_cons: Quick feet for a big nose tackle. Can play any interior alignment in an odd front. Solid pursuit speed for a player of his size. Plays on the ground/on his knees too much. Block-shed ability falls off quickly if his first move fails. Noticeably short arms make it tough for him to get off blocks.

summary: Collins is a former five-star recruit from Bastrop, Texas, where he competed in football, basketball and track (shot put and discus). As a true freshman in college, he played in 10 games but made just one start, a theme that continued for most of his Longhorns career. That changed in 2024 when Collins stepped into a full- time starting role and became a positive presence. At 6-foot-5 and 315 pounds, Collins now profiles more as an interior defensive lineman than an edge. He has good length for an interior player, paired with a strong upper body and powerful hands that allow him to dictate stack-and-shed moves and fight through double teams. However, his height and length also present challenges, as he naturally struggles with leverage. His biggest drawback is how slow he can be to disengage. It's not that he can’t shed blockers, but rather that he lacks urgency. A quicker processing speed in this area would make him a more impactful pass rusher.
pros_and_cons: Excellent length for an interior defensive lineman. Strong upper body with an effective long-arm move. Well-built frame with good lower-body weight distribution. Violent, powerful hands to control blockers. Strong enough to fight through double teams. Lacks pursuit speed on plays outside the tackles. Can be slow to disengage and shed blocks. Naturally plays with a high pad level.

summary: Farmer was a three-star recruit in the 2021 class. While the 250- pounder was seen as too small to play defensive line full time in Division I, he committed to Florida State and has put on a good 60 pounds to now look and play like a stout defensive tackle. He was a consistent starter over the past two seasons. First-step explosiveness is important for trench players, but Farmer also has impressive burst and acceleration on his second and third steps. That allows him to create a strong pop at contact. He has good flexibility and a naturally low pad level to maintain good leverage out of his pre-snap stance. He also brings uniquely long arms and large hands for the position. Farmer’s pass-rush wins are often a result of those first few explosive steps, lacking many true finesse wins with moves and a plan. He is strong in the run game but too easily gets walled off and moved out of his gap. He projects as a rotational player with the athletic build to be more.
pros_and_cons: Low pad level in his stance and after the snap. Good pop at contact to knock back blockers. Plus arm length for an interior defender. First few steps have impressive explosiveness. Needs a deeper pass-rush bag. Could stand to make a rip move more of a constant finisher. Gets walled off/angled too easily in run defense.

summary: Graham was a four-star recruit and a two-time state champion wrestler. He initially wanted to play linebacker, but his coach convinced him his best shot at a top Division I offer and the NFL was in the trenches. His PFF pass-rush grade on true pass sets, PFF run-defense grade, pass-rush win rate and solo run-stop rate over the past two years at Michigan are all above the 95th percentile. He has adequate size to play 3-technique in the NFL, but he played at just about every alignment on the defensive front over the past two years. Graham is explosive in his first step, giving him good speed-to-power conversion and effective push- pull moves. He shows good bend, and his hands are fast, violent and well placed, especially in run defense. He likes to use a two- hand swipe or a club-arm over as his main pass-rush moves. His biggest issues stem from a lack of arm length, but there is still so much to like. His competitive toughness and motor are ideal.
pros_and_cons: Elite first-step explosiveness. Excellent bend and flexibility for an interior player. Wins the leverage battle consistently. Fast, powerful hands. Devastating push-pull move. Arms appear to be well below average. Lack of length affects rip/swipe efficiency. Shorter arms make it tougher for him to disengage.

summary: Grant is a former four-star recruit from Merrillville, Indiana. In high school, he played on both sides of the ball as a guard and defensive tackle while also competing in the shot put in track and field. At Michigan, he has played exclusively on the defensive line, serving as a reserve in 2022 before becoming a full-time starter in 2023 and 2024. Grant has ideal size for the nose tackle position, standing 6-foot-3 and weighing nearly 340 pounds. He also possesses rare quickness for his size. That quickness flashes in pure pass-rush situations and when shooting gaps. His hand speed can match his lower-body quickness, but not always. Too often, his hands are slow or appear flailing. His biggest issue is that he isn’t always in attack mode. While some of his assignments involve looping or containing, there are too many snaps where he hesitates rather than attacks. When he does play with aggression, he is a force.
pros_and_cons: Exceptional quickness for a player of his size. Quick to counter moves and adjust mid-rush. Active hands in passing lanes, leading to batted passes. Impressive overall athleticism for his frame. Executes E-T stunts effectively when looping inside. Plays too high at times, losing leverage. Hand usage can be erratic and lack purpose. Accuracy numbers are high, but ball placement isn't consistent.

summary: Harmon committed to Michigan State as a three-star recruit, and after redshirting his first season, he was a rotational starter in 2022 and a full-time starter in 2023 before transferring to Oregon. Harmon wins with quickness — a quick first step, quick hands into the body and an ability to dictate contact. He can get low and maintain a low pad level in a four-point stance, but his high- waisted build is more obvious in a three-point stance, making it tough for him to get low and not pop up immediately after the snap. He pairs his long arms with upper-tier hand speed to make initial contact or execute a pass-rush move. He always finishes his gap-shooting and cross-face moves with a rip to get clean. His hand work is where he disrupts; he is difficult to stay in front of and latched onto. He displays a high football IQ and the why of defensive line play. Harmon constantly communicates pre-snap and has a good motor and a competitive attitude through the whistle.
pros_and_cons: Good arm length for the interior. Quick first step and quick footwork. Fast hands off the snap to get inside and dictate first moves. Push-pull and arm-over moves are natural and smooth. Competitive player with a good motor. Build is naturally a little high-waisted. Pops up and loses leverage out of his stance. Lighter in the lower half at current weight.

summary: At 6-foot-6 and 280 pounds, he is built for the NFL. His size and strength create versatility as a defensive end in odd or even fronts. He doesn't have a ton of pass-rush moves, but the ones he does know (bull rush, swim, club-rip) can be very effective, especially anything with a club-arm over that he pairs with getting across a blocker's face. His punch at contact is imposing for just about anyone. He generates a crazy amount of power and movement from his hands when bull rushing and stacking blocks. He doesn't have rare first-step explosiveness to really threaten the outside shoulder, so he would likely fit best sliding inside to a 3-4 defensive end. He must continue to improve anticipating blocks. If he can do that, he might just become unblockable.
pros_and_cons: Naturally one of the strongest DL on the field. Has the size to play inside and out along the DL. Quick hands, especially when executing an arm-over move. Has the power to square up OTs and hold POA versus the run. Long arms to create PBUs in the throwing window. Need to anticipate blockers/contact better. Pops up and loses leverage almost immediately out of stance. Can get bounced around as blockers can get under his pads.

summary: Originally a four-star recruit from Louisiana, Jones chose to stay in his home state over offers from Ole Miss, Texas A&M and others. After seeing action in a rotational role as a freshman and sophomore, he became a full-time starter in 2023 and had his best year yet as a senior this past season. His 43 pressures were tied for eighth among all edge defenders in the SEC. While Jones was primarily an edge for the Tigers, he's able to line up anywhere on the defensive line at 6-foot-5, 280 pounds. He pairs that size with a motor that never quits while having solid tools at that size. While Jones employs multiple pass-rushing moves, his hand usage is still relatively unrefined. He also could afford to be more physical in the run game as he gets washed out of plays far too often right now.
pros_and_cons: Can win from both a two-point and three-point stance. Relentless motor shows maximum effort on every play. Adequate length with good power and bend as a pass-rusher. Explosive first-step at 280 pounds. Needs to work on his hand usage as a pass-rusher. Has had tackling issues due to playing off balance. Not a very stout run-defender routinely gets washed out of plays.

summary: At 6-foot-5, 295 pounds, Mills is lean but long. This makes him an easier projection to a 3-4 defensive end spot due to his versatility in his build (length to play more of a defensive end spot, weight to hold up well enough on the inside). He is a better pass-rusher than he is a run defender. He has a quick first step and active, violent hands to stay clean when shooting gaps. He does struggle to get off blocks if he doesn't win early. He can play with a high pad level, which limits his efficacy when anchoring against the run. His pass-rush win percentage will be one of the higher marks of the interior defensive line class thanks to a well- executed long arm, club-rip and bull rush (though his leg drive can die out quickly). He has long arms to bat down passes in throwing windows. He also has good lateral quickness for stunts as a crasher or looper. As a whole, he plays with a good motor for all four quarters.
pros_and_cons: Shows good strength and instinct to stack and shed blocks. Hands are strong and violent. Good lateral quickness for stunts. Has the length to play almost any defensive line spot. Long arms to get in passing lanes for PBUs. Hands are violent but out of control at times. Naturally high pad level. Must play more in control/balanced.

summary: Nolen was a five-star recruit and the No. 2 player in the 2022 class, according to 247Sports. He started his college career at Texas A&M as a rotational defensive lineman for two years before transferring to Ole Miss and becoming a consensus All- American in 2024. At 6-foot-3 and 295 pounds, Nolen has so much natural power. His upper body is incredibly strong, helping him throw off blockers or crash through double teams. Because of that, he is an impactful run defender. If Nolen doesn't win with his first step or speed-to-power bull rush, his efforts can stall. He also relies too much on power to fight through once blocked. His hand usage improved in 2024 but needs more precision and purpose. That would also help him not expose his chest as much to linemen. He got better in all those areas from 2023 to 2024, but more growth is needed. Nolen has long arms (67th percentile), giving him some positional versatility, but he will be best as a 3- technique in the NFL.
pros_and_cons: Incredibly strong, especially with momentum. Clear raw strength and explosiveness. Has the build to play defensive end and defensive tackle. Very strong tackler with a low missed tackle rate. Good effort to the whistle. Needs to be more purposeful, but looked less reckless in 2024. Lacks a go-to pass-rush move. Exposes his chest too easily.

summary: Norman-Lott was a spot starter in 2022 at Arizona State before transferring to Tennessee, where he featured in a deep defensive line rotation over the past two seasons. The Volunteers rotated their linemen constantly, causing Norman-Lott to record less than 500 snaps over the past two years. He has a strong first step that converts speed to power easily. His shorter stature gives him leverage out of three- and four-point stances. He has above- average arms for bull rushes and massive hands to strike with power at his punches. He wins primarily with athleticism and some surprising flexibility and agility, but his game lacks technique. Too often he approaches pass rushing with a hesitation move that lacks purpose. Yet, he recorded a high pass-rush win rate because of the violence and speed in his hands, as well as his burst. He is strong at around 300 pounds and can take on double teams decently well, but he will need better technique to do so in the NFL.
pros_and_cons: Explosive and powerful 3-technique. Natural four-point stance rusher with great leverage off snap. Impressive upper-body strength to bench press linemen back. Surprising flexibility and bend for an interior player. Massive hands and above-average arm length. Needs more of a pass-rush plan. Lower measurables in height and weight. Freelances too much as a run defender.

summary: Peebles, a three-star recruit, committed to Duke and was more of a spot starter and rotational player in four seasons with the Blue Devils. But at Virginia Tech in 2024, he was a starter and one of the top defensive linemen in college football. Peebles’ measurables won't do him any favors — sub-10th percentile in height, weight and arm length — but his film is better than that. He has a stocky build with a quick first step and purposeful hands off the line of scrimmage. He brings a good game plan at the snap, but if his first move doesn't hit, his effectiveness can stall. He is a high-effort player and always looks to get closer to the ball until the whistle. He has a solid bag of pass-rush moves, including a shoulder dip and spin move.
