He shows good instincts for the snap count and where the ball is going through play action or pre-snap motion. He struggles with power aspects, but if he can avoid those situations more often than not, he can be a solid pro.
pros_and_cons: Quickness is his calling card. Instinctive to dip his shoulder when cornering. Good eyes for where the ball is going. Effective hand placement and arm extension to maintain control. High-effort player. Low weight percentile shows up when taking on combo blocks. Struggles to shed blocks once linemen get hands on him. Can look a little off balance when going all out to match power.

summary: The word to describe Pegues is versatile. He was originally a four- star tight end coming out of Oxford, Mississippi and chose to play at Auburn over his hometown school, Ole Miss. After spending a year as a tight end with the Tigers, he made the move over to defense for his sophomore season. He then came back home to play for the Rebels for his final three years. Pegues isn't a versatile player only due to his ability to play on two sides of the ball, he's versatile because he played all along Ole Miss' defensive line. He has excellent agility at over 300 pounds which allows him to win on the interior or on the edge. Pegues is still learning how to play defense, which is evident by his slow reaction time on some runs. He also doesn't have great length or pad level right now. And hey, if a career at defensive tackle doesn't work out, he could always play fullback.
pros_and_cons: Elite quickness and change-of-direction ability. Versatile player who won both on the interior and on the edge. Pops offensive linemen on first contact. Was a weapon as a blocker and even as a ball-carrier. Can get too upright at times. Still reacting more than anticipating as processing speed lags. Doesn't have great length and didn’t test well.

summary: Phillips is a former three-star recruit from Ocoee, Florida, who was also a standout weightlifter and wrestler. He initially signed with Tennessee in the 2022 recruiting class but transferred to Maryland after redshirting, where he became a full-time starter for two seasons. He will be one of the youngest players in the class, having declared with multiple years of eligibility remaining. Phillips was ranked No. 51 on Bruce Feldman’s College Football Freaks list, boasting a 665-pound squat, 365-pound power clean and the ability to overhead press 365 pounds for two reps. That power translates to the field, where he is incredibly strong at holding the point of attack. He is below the 20th percentile in height, hand size and arm length. However, his strength and explosiveness compensate for those deficiencies. Even in his current form, he is already a pro-caliber run defender at nose tackle.
pros_and_cons: Low, loaded and wide pre-snap stance provides a strong base. Well-built frame with no obvious weaknesses in size or strength. Carries significant weight and power in his lower half. Lack of arm length makes it difficult to disengage from blockers. Lacks pass-rusher’s mentality, limiting his impact as a disruptor.

summary: He is built very well at 290 pounds with hand size and arm length in the 60th percentile for the defensive end position. He is a tad shorter, and that, plus his sub-34-inch reach, makes me believe playing more of an interior defensive end spot could be best for him in the NFL. He not only has experience but also successfully aligned anywhere from a 4i DE to a wide-7 OLB. He is explosive, especially when adjusting his speed with his size, but I wouldn't say he is twitchy. He uses a variety of pass-rush moves, but they don't always result in the cleanest wins. He also struggles to get off blocks once linemen get in front of him. His linear explosiveness off the line is good, but his later movements can look slow, and overall, he lacks the bend needed to win as a full- time edge.
pros_and_cons: Dense, powerful defensive lineman. Has experience and success at many spots on the DL. Explosive for his size. Can be slow to recognize/anticipate misdirection plays. Lateral stop-and-start can be stiff/slow. Lacks the bend to be considered a full-time edge defender.

summary: Sanders played defensive line and tight end in high school while also shining in basketball. He ultimately pursued football and committed to South Carolina. He was a rotational player in 2022 before starting in 2023 and 2024. The 6-foot-3 ½, 290-pound interior defender wins with a quick first step and a knack for shooting gaps. He crosses up linemen with unique lateral quickness and has longer arms, well above the 50th percentile for the position, to help him bat passes. His PFF pass-rush grades are high, but his true win rate is low because he often generated pressure with his first step and long arms but lacked the strength and precise hands to win cleanly. Sanders has a variety of pass- rush moves, but his hand placement is inconsistent. He can hold the line in two-gap situations but, for the most part, is pushed off the ball by NFL-level strength. He is an unreliable tackler, too often diving at ankles. His motor runs hot, especially on key downs.
pros_and_cons: Quick hands to engage and get off blocks. Plus arm length for the interior. Explosive first step laterally and linearly. Has some twitch for 290-pounder. Long arms for pass breakups. Gives up leverage quickly post-snap. Can get overzealous to shoot a gap in run defense. Does not hold up well against doubles.

summary: Smith committed to Alabama over Florida, Miami, Clemson and others. He was a depth defensive lineman as a true freshman but worked his way up and started 13 games in 2024. At just over 6- foot-4 and 311 pounds, Smith brings ideal size for the NFL. His arm length is also right around the 50th percentile. Pass rushing won't be Smith’s strong suit in the league. His pass-rush win rate was never above 8.0% in a season, and he lacks the requisite first-step explosiveness. That also limits his speed-to-power conversion on bull rushes. He is reliable as a run defender with decently high marks in that facet over his final two seasons, but his lack of pop at contact shows up there, as well. He has good grip strength to stack and shed versus the run, showcasing that best against Michigan in the ReliaQuest Bowl to end the 2024 season.
pros_and_cons: Well-built interior defender. Low pad level in his preferred four-point stance. Big, strong hands that consistently hit aiming points. Played everything from 0-technique to 4i defensive end. Plays off balance/on the ground too much. Middling first-step explosiveness. Strength is decent but not difference-making.

summary: Tafuna, a former high school linebacker, bulked up from 225 pounds in his recruiting days to more than 300 pounds now as a defensive tackle. He recorded 45 starts at the position over the past four years at Utah. His linebacker background gives him unique quickness, laterally and up the field. He can shoot gaps and catch offensive linemen off guard by how quickly he gets across their faces. Tafuna also shows active hands to stay clean throughout a rep, which is important because his strength and speed often die out after those first few steps. His linebacker history provides him with good pursuit speed, tackling fundamentals and a strong feel for where the ball is going. However, he still lacks the overall build for an NFL defensive tackle. It is a challenge for him to hold up against double teams and just play with the anchor often required to be a full-time defensive tackle. His effort is consistently high, though, which should help him stick on a roster.
pros_and_cons: Unique first-step quickness for an interior defender. Good lateral movements to get across the face of blockers. Hands are up and active to keep his chest clean. Quick reaction time to cut blocks and swing passes. Good pursuit speed. Doesn't have the best build for a defensive tackle in the NFL. Power dies out quickly if he doesn't shoot a gap cleanly.

summary: Turner was a four-star recruit in the 2021 class. He played in eight games as a true freshman at Texas A&M in 2021 before starting in his last three college seasons. He is listed at 6-foot-4 and 300 pounds but appears to be on the smaller side for an NFL defensive lineman, specifically in arm length. What Turner lacks in length he makes up for in hand usage and effort. His hands are active and fast to swipe and chop off the snap, helping him stay clean or fight through with counters to disengage. His consistent leverage allows him to hold the line of scrimmage well in run defense, and his active, strong hands give him the upper hand to stack and shed when the ball carrier arrives. He likes to use a swim/arm-over move to shoot gaps, but his arm length can stop him from winning cleanly. Turner can also struggle to hold his own against double teams, making it tough to say he will be truly versatile in the NFL despite his experience at 0-1-technique nose tackle.
pros_and_cons: High-motor player. Fast, active hands. Good instincts for where the ball is going. Lower weight profile so he gets pushed around vs. doubles. Seems to have shorter arms than his frame indicates.

summary: Walker’s measurables land in the 90th percentile or above in height, weight, hand size and arm length. His sheer mass makes him a daunting assignment for an interior offensive lineman, and he has some unique quickness at his size. His build also gives him versatility for odd and even fronts. He has quick hands and a nice club-arm over off the snap as a go-to, but overall, he needs more precision in his pass-rush moves. He tips the scale, but his weight distribution is to his disadvantage. He carries a good amount of his weight in his midsection, and his calves/ankles are narrow. This, along with him tending to pop up right out of his stance, makes him easier to move, especially when being pushed laterally. He gives good effort for a big man and loves to get his long arms up for PBUs.
pros_and_cons: Very quick first step for a player of his size. Possesses a baseline for a variety of pass-rush moves. Has the length to play 3-4 DE. Hand usage is quick despite also very long length. Good natural power in his upper body. Not a lot of weight in his lower half despite weighing 340 pounds. High-waisted so tougher for him to sit in his stance. Pops up quickly out of his stance.

summary: West is on the smaller side for an NFL defensive tackle (length- wise) at just over 6-foot-1 with 31 1/2-inch arms, both ranking below the 10th percentile. But you don't have to worry about mass, as he plays around 315 pounds, which is more than adequate for the position. He has a quick first step and a high- energy style that makes him tough to stay in front of in pass-rush situations. He can stop, start and explode in linear movements upfield and lateral movements when shuffling along the line. His active hands help him hit moves and get clean. He can also slice through gaps like butter, usually combining his first step with a swim/arm-over move. He has impressive strength to two-gap when needed. For a player who should always win the leverage battle, West gives up his leverage superiority too often. His shorter arms also impact his ability to wrap up and make plays in the backfield. His motor runs hot, so effort should not be a question.
pros_and_cons: High-energy play style makes it tough to keep him blocked. Good first-step explosiveness to set up vs. run and pass. Explosive in linear and lateral movements. Quick, strong, active hands. Can knife through a gap like butter. Could use more violence in his club move. Gives up leverage quicker than you want for a smaller DT. Shorter arms for an NFL DT.

summary: Williams is a former four-star defensive tackle recruit from Manassas, VA. He didn’t play his senior year of high school after Virginia canceled the season due to COVID-19, and by his own admission, he let himself go. When he enrolled at Ohio State, he weighed 360 pounds, but after reshaping his body to a more controlled 325-330 pounds, he became a much more consistent player. Williams was a rotational player in 2021 and 2022 before becoming a full-time starter in 2023 and 2024. His calling card is his power. He plays with a compact, explosive stance that allows him to fire off the ball and convert speed to power. He has the frame to play both interior spots (nose and 3-tech), but his skill set is best suited for a run-stuffing nose tackle role. However, he lacks a well-developed pass-rush arsenal. His career pass-rush win rate has remained below 10.0%, and he doesn’t showcase many finesse moves. If he doesn’t win with his first step, his rushes tend to stall out.
pros_and_cons: Compact, powerful stance pre-snap for a strong base. Versatile frame to play both nose tackle and 3-technique. Explosive first step to shoot gaps and generate power. Vastly improved hand speed, precision, and purpose in 2024. Effective corkscrew technique to hold up against double teams. Tends to pop up too quickly, causing him to lose leverage. Struggles to hold ground against combo blocks. Needs to develop a deeper arsenal of pass-rush moves.

summary: Baron is a former 4-star defensive end recruit from Knoxville, Tennessee. He first attended The Ensworth School in Nashville, Tennessee, before transferring to Knoxville Catholic High School back in Knoxville. He then committed to stay close to home at UT, playing as a spot starter for his first three seasons until becoming a regular starter in 2023. He then chose to transfer to Miami for his final year in 2024. Overall his game seems to lack some strength and violence to take his all-around ability to an impactful level. His speed-to-power conversion is middling and stalls out too quickly, even against tight ends. His missed tackle percentage shot up in 2024, and there just seems to be a lack of density and power when he's hitting.
pros_and_cons: NFL caliber frame in both height and weight. Good natural athlete with balance, strength and speed. Consistent leg drive for bull rushes and getting off blocks. Decent agility to cross face of blockers. Too many snaps he has a false start or doesn't fire off his front foot. Pass rush moves lack precision and purpose right now. Needs to develop more counters to get off blocks quicker.

summary: His 6-foot-5, 290-pound measurables give him true scheme versatility, which he shows in his tape, aligning anywhere from a 3-technique defensive tackle to a 7-technique outside linebacker. After re-shaping his body in the summer of 2024, he currently has his best combination of size, speed and strength (which has been a journey to find the sweet spot throughout his career). He has always been a very good weight-adjusted athlete and continues to be, winning with a nice first step and good leg drive as a pass- rusher. Right now, his game lacks a consistent approach for a pass rush plan — the ball will be snapped before he'll fire off the line and not know which move he'll throw (too often not throwing one). Though he has a strong first step, he lacks the bend and flexibility to be a constant threat to the outside shoulder. He is improving as a passer-rusher, though, as 2024 was by far his most effective year in that category. He is a decent run defender but could stand to have a high floor.
pros_and_cons: Great measurables for the edge position. Scheme versatile defender who can play multiple positions. Frame is well filled out for all that height and weight. Very nice first-step explosiveness for his size. Extremely low missed tackle percentage. Needs more of a pass rush plan before the ball is snapped. Hands lack purpose. Lacks the bend to truly threaten the outside shoulder with speed.

summary: At 6-foot-3 and 255 pounds, it is hard not to see another former No.11 from Penn State (Micah Parsons) in his play. Carter is incredibly explosive in his movements and has some of the best bend, not just in this class but in the NFL. He has a very explosive and violent rip move. His speed-to-power conversion allows him to be a decently high-floor run defender, though he might struggle there early on as he acclimates to NFL size and strength. He does have shorter arms for an edge rusher. This impacts his ability to stack and shed, fully disengage from blocks, get his hands up in passing lanes and wrap up QBs. His pass-rush bag, as expected, is a work in progress, as 2024 was his first year as a full-time edge rusher. His hand usage and effectiveness only improved as the year went on. He has the build of an OLB pass- rusher, but if his weight is right, he could succeed as a 4-3 edge as well.
pros_and_cons: Rare athlete for the position — Tier 1 NFL speed. Natural explosiveness and bend are both elite. Willingness to play physical despite lighter weight. Pass rushes like a basketball guard — cross over style. Good speed-to-power conversion for a player of his size. Has a small false step. Arms will likely be on the shorter side. Can lead with the shoulder too often when taking on puller.

summary: Ezeiruaku is smaller for an NFL edge rusher at just over 6-foot-2 and around 240 pounds. Without an elite first step, he fails to converge speed-to-power to really boast a strong bull rush or long arm. He also isn't very dense when trying to hold the point of attack in traditional run defense assignments. His first step might not be the most explosive, but it is quick and smooth into his top speed. He also has some very impressive bend to execute dip-rip moves as well as cross chop moves with precision and effectiveness. His hand usage is fast and precise to stay clean, and he consistently maximizes leverage with good pad level and long arms. He is a high IQ player with great eyes for the ball. He is also very sound as a tackler with a low missed tackle percentage. He might not be able to hold the point of attack great when square to the line of scrimmage, but when given the freedom to defend the run by attacking, he has graded very well defending the run.
pros_and_cons: First step is both explosive and smooth. His arm length can be an advantage and uses it consistently. Maximizes leverage to make up for lack of weight. Good eyes and anticipation for the ball. Very sound tackler with a very low missed tackle percentage. Tough for him to take on pullers and lead blockers. Pursuit speed and explosiveness are average-to-below average. Does not convert speed-to-power in an imposing manner.

summary: He is small at just over 6-foot-2, but he is strong as an ox at 265 pounds — he weighed 220 pounds as a recruit. He carries a lot of his mass in his quads, hamstrings and glutes, which manifests into a very strong leg drive when bull rushing and anchoring versus the run. He has a physical play style — every time the ball is snapped, he looks to make contact. He likes a long arm move to get blockers on their heels, but his lack of arm length (well below average) limits how effective it is past initial contact. His hands are fast and violent, but the lack of length makes it tough for him to get off blocks, even with his relentlessness. Pound-for- pound, he is an impressive run defender and can even slide into play 3-technique or 4i defensive tackle. His pass-rush win percentage and pressure numbers are high, but he doesn't turn those into sacks at a high rate.
pros_and_cons: Good weight in lower half for strong leg drive. Lacks height but consistently wins leverage battle. Good first-step explosiveness with no false steps. Has a physical mentality needed for trench play. Hands are violent when he throws any sort of chop or swipe. Likes to push his blockers but needs to get off blocks quicker. Hands are fast but not precise. Arm length will be below the threshold for some teams.

summary: Listed at 6-foot-4, 248 pounds, he has a nice first step and some twitchy change of direction suddenness. Green’s hand usage and pass-rush moves aren't mastered yet, but there is a lot of potential in the speed and violence with which he attempts his moves. He is also constantly working to get free if his initial move doesn't work. He has a nice cross chop move he likes to go to, and he has a few snaps where his spin move is devastating. He needs to make sure he is launching off his front foot with no false step to improve his first-step effectiveness even more. He is also a stout run defender at sub-250 pounds to project as a full-time edge defender. His hands, which fast, can be a bit reckless with plenty of reps where he is hitting and grabbing the face of his blocker, and he needs to keep his eyes up to make sure he sees what he hits — since he's not shy for physical play.
pros_and_cons: Adequate length for the position at the NFL level (long arms). Well built and balanced. Explosive first step to threaten OT's balance and quickness. Good lateral quickness to shoot gaps inside. Always working to get clean, even if he hasn't mastered how yet. Launching off his back foot could help when attacking outside. Needs to keep his eyes up consistently when making contact. Hands can be high and get up into the facemask of blockers.

summary: Despite lacking ideal height and length, Hassanein is well built and plays stronger than his listed size would suggest, largely due to his excellent leverage and pad level. He lacks the first-step quickness needed to penetrate gaps or win the edge, but he can defeat blockers quickly with heavy and quick hands. He plays with a relentless motor and will give maximum effort on every down, allowing him to be an effective clean-up player in pursuit. While he is very adept at defeating blocks at the line of scrimmage, Hassanein doesn't finish as many plays as he should because he tends to lunge at the ball carrier instead of staying on his feet to drive through and wrap up his target. His lack of length is a concern against bigger NFL linemen, and he was too easily displaced when trying to slant into gaps as opposed to engaging blockers head-up.
pros_and_cons: Wins at line of scrimmage with pad level and hand usage. Stays square to line of scrimmage and in position. Works hard to shed blocks and win gaps. 27 bench reps at combine translates to field. High-motor guy, plays through whistle and chases plays down. Doesn’t have ideal NFL length. Gets washed out too easily when not engaging his blocker. Needs a better assortment of pass-rush moves.

summary: At just under 6-foot-6 and 270 pounds, he has the size to play in odd and even fronts on the defensive line. One of his go-to moves is a cross chop that he finishes with a rip move. He also likes to use a long arm move to get linemen on their heels, and he can also hit a two-hand swipe cleanly. He has a large tackling radius and a low missed tackle percentage over the last two seasons. He is sound defending the run — wins with leverage, gets his hands inside and arms fully extended and keeps his shoulders square with his eyes on the ball to read at the right time. He has some snaps where he shows off more flexibility and bend than expected for his regular game and size — though overall, he does lack some agility to be a top-tier pass-rusher. His first-step explosiveness is decent but is more build-up than twitched-up. As much as he is a hard worker, he is also smart. He has a good understanding of where the ball is going and when it is being snapped.
pros_and_cons: Height, weight and length above 90th percentile for edge. Adequate strength to hold the line and take on pulling blockers. Surprising flexibility (at times) for his size. Maintains good leverage despite taller frame. Long arms make for an extensive tackling radius. Injury history that includes two ACL injuries. Larger frame limits twitch/change of direction. First step is decent, but his speed is more build up.

summary: Kennard’s arm length looks like a plus, even beyond his 6-foot-5 height. He has a good understanding of pass-rush plans. He has a good variety of pass-rush moves that involve crossing face, single-arm chops and rips, push-pull moves as well as outside attacks, too. As a run defender, he is aggressive in shooting gaps and getting to landmarks when slanting or versus zone, but his leaner frame does give him trouble to really hold the point of attack. His fundamentals show a great baseline. He rarely has any false steps out of his stance, consistently launching off the front foot. His hands are always active to stay clean, and he is a reliable tackler. When he rushes from a two-point stance, he can lose the leverage battle pretty easily. The only thing really holding him back from a very high grade is that his athleticism and flexibility are good but not elite.
pros_and_cons: Explosive first step — good speed-to-power rusher. Zero wasted steps in his rush up the arc. Very fast hands make him tough to stay in front of. Looks to have plus arm length for the position. Good bag of initial pass rush moves. Naturally rushes high from a two-point stance. Needs to develop more counters when the first move fails. Lean frame.

summary: Oladejo was a three-star prospect who played his first two college seasons at Cal in an off-ball linebacker role. He improved his PFF defensive grade each year in college, from 54.8 in 2021 to 56.4 in 2022 to 70.9 in 2023 to 73.8 in 2024. After two seasons with the Golden Bears, Oladejo transferred to UCLA. It wasn’t until two games into his senior season with the Bruins that he played the majority of his snaps in an edge role, so he lacks experience and a fully formed pass-rush repertoire. Oladejo impressed at Senior Bowl practices by winning the majority of his pass-rush one-on- one reps. He is an inexperienced pass-rusher that teams will want to take a chance on due to his athleticism and 33 3/8-inch arms.
pros_and_cons: Wins with athleticism and quickness as a run defender. Plays with effort to the whistle. Long arms keep blockers at a distance. Positional versatility and can play off-ball LB or on the edge. Overeager when tracking the ball carrier and gets out of his gap. Still inexperienced at the edge position with only 10 starts. Not a fully polished pass-rusher yet.

summary: Pearce has one of the quickest first steps you'll see of any rusher in this class and others. His feet fire fast, as do his hands. He can knock away offensive linemen's punches and has incredibly quick club, swipe and rip moves to get around the outside shoulder. He is not only very twitchy in his movements but also flexible, as he can get down in a 3/4-point stance and fire off the ball with leverage, though he does look more natural as a 2-point standout outside linebacker. As a run defender, he can get handled one-on-one against tackles and tight ends, but he does have some good speed-to-power pop versus the run. Though his pass-rush grade and win percentages are both already very high, he could have a true pass-rush plan more consistently. He could also more consistently launch off his front foot. His snap count is lower than most of his peers due to Tennessee's hockey-like defensive line lines that they would rotate throughout games.
pros_and_cons: Very twitchy player with an explosive first step. Decent speed-to-power punch given his low weight. Good anticipation for snap count/appropriate pre-snap shifts. Knows how to attack the half-man consistently. Excellent pursuit speed to the ball carrier. Light weight makes it easier to lock him up/get him to the ground. Not much flexibility to play him anywhere inside 5-tech. Need more of a true pass-rush plan more often.

summary: His shorter stature (6-foot-2, 240 pounds) does impact how well he can get off blocks and hold the line in run defense, but it also makes him a quick and explosive player. His speed and strength shine brightest when in a standup 3-4 OLB alignment where he can angle himself toward the pocket. His hand speed and precision are easy to love — his swipes, club and rip moves are very fast and allow him to stay clean up the arc when attacking the outside shoulder. In run defense, his initial first step gives him a good pop at contact thanks to speed-to-power conversion, but his leg drive quickly dies out after that. He also lacks the consistent leverage to be surprisingly strong and durable in true run defense assignments. His pass-rush bag is pretty deep headed into the NFL, led by a strong and effective spin move.
pros_and_cons: More compact frame does give him some good power/burst. Powerful spin move that he uses at the right times. Hand usage is generally precise and effective with leverage. Very fast hands for swipes, clubs and rips to stay clean. Shorter strides limit how much ground he covers. Lower percentile arm length does show up against NFL-level OTs. Lack of arm length limits pass-rush moves.

summary: Robinson, after playing mainly behind Will Anderson Jr., Chris Braswell and Dallas Turner in a talented edge room, got his chance to start at Alabama as a redshirt senior in 2024. He played in just nine games, missing the rest due to an elbow injury, and recorded only 341 snaps over the past two years. At 6-foot-4 with 33 1/2-inch arms, he brings adequate NFL height and length to the edge. His weight (around 243 pounds) is lighter than ideal, but he plays strong. His first-step explosiveness was the catalyst for a 19.0% pass-rush win rate over the past two seasons. That speed rush can be even better if he becomes comfortable firing off his front foot instead of his back foot in his stance. Robinson’s game lacks diversity. He has a strong long-arm move, but he doesn't have much of a pass-rush plan aside from winning with speed and length. His lateral quickness is effective, but his bend is a bit stiff for being just a speed rusher.
pros_and_cons: Ideal height and length for the NFL. Length gives him an advantage with stack and shed. Most comfortable rushing from a two-point stance. Very good first-step burst. Pound-for-pound a strong player. Lack of weight/leverage shows up in negative run-defense plays. Lacks top-level flexibility/bend. Still raw in overall anticipation and pass-rush moves/timing.

summary: Rucker brings a stronger bull rush than you'd expect for a player who is under 6-foot-2, though he weighs around 255 pounds. He is a fundamentally sound player with precise hands, square shoulders to the LOS and good eyes into the backfield. His pass- rush plan feels well thought out and with purpose. He is also a natural mover, so teams can feel comfortable spot-dropping him into zone coverage every now and then. His pass-rush scores were high, including a 93rd-percentile win percentage, though his sack production was low throughout his career. He also seems like a guy who just loves football — he talked about how happy he was to just put on his uniform again to play on nine snaps the first game back from injury. He is also a reliable tackler with a low missed tackle percentage.
pros_and_cons: Active hands are always trying to keep him clean. Packs a punch at contact due to his frame and natural leverage. Has decent burst and bend on passing downs. Sound tackler with good tackling technique. Natural movement skills as a drop zone defender. Short strides don't cover a ton of ground in pursuit. Change of direction is a bit stiff/doesn't cover a lot of ground. Unsure he has the frame to be more than a pass rush specialist.

summary: He has high grades defending the run and rushing the passer over the last two seasons, and he has a 6-foot-5, 265-pound frame to project a high floor at the NFL level. He has a strong first step that is consistently clean off his front foot with no false steps as a pass-rusher. He also has good speed-to-power conversion and bases most of his pass rush success around a bull rush. He has a developing spin move and two-handed swipe but is still working on hitting them cleanly. He has good length, strength and hand technique to consistently stack and shed on his terms and quickly. He also has long arms and a good feel for when the ball is coming out to get his hands up for PBUs. He is also a good enough athlete to spot-drop into coverage a handful of times per game. He is a consistent competitor with a good motor.
pros_and_cons: Good eyes, timing and strength to stack and shed against run. First step is consistently from the front foot in his stance. Fundamentally sound player who is rarely out of position. Good feel for when and where passes are going to get PBUs. Athletic enough to spot-drop from an edge spot in coverage. Needs a deeper pass rush bag beyond power moves. Not a bendy pass-rusher on the outside. Arms are average to below average.

summary: He's listed at 6-foot-4, 280 pounds. That size profile gives him the ability to line up anywhere from a 4i DE to a 7-tech OLB. He has a strong upper body but plays with high pad leverage when aligned as an OLB — naturally better from three-point stance. At Purdue, he showed a wide variety of pass-rush moves, both in power and finesse. He also has a really nice spin move that he goes to when tackles over set to the outside. In 2024, we didn't see all those moves as much or as effectively, but they are still there. His hand work is fast but felt more ineffective this season when it came to staying clean and truly winning a rep. He also seems to lack the flexibility to really turn the corner at a high level, which is understandable given his size. His frame gives him a good ability to anchor versus the run, though he would rather defend the run by attacking the backfield. His arm length appears to be below average for the NFL, which shows up in some difficulty getting off blocks when OL get hands on him.
pros_and_cons: Carries 280 pounds very well for an edge who can be OLB or DE. Experience playing both right and left side of the line. Many pass-rush moves already feel like second nature. Has a natural instinct to swipe his hands and stay clean. Comfortable shallow zone dropping from OLB spot. Isn't as violent defending the run as he could be. Loads/launches off his back foot. Plays with high pad level.

summary: Stewart is smaller for full-time edge work in the NFL, listed at 6- foot-1 and 242 pounds. However, he packs a punch at contact with good leverage despite those deficiencies. He is explosive and consistently launches off the front foot to give himself the best chance to beat blockers to the outside. His hands are fast, but they can be purposeless at times. Right now, he primarily wins due to a great first step with good leverage and high effort. He doesn't have a lot of pass-rush moves. On the line of scrimmage, he can get handled one-on-one in the run game, but then there are other reps where he'll give you a surprising win versus a player much bigger than him. He is strong as a tackler, though his tackle radius is smaller. He honestly feels like a player who might be more of an off-ball linebacker than an edge rusher when it comes to an NFL projection.
pros_and_cons: Not afraid to be physical despite smaller stature. All-around explosive athlete. Can attack both shoulders when aligned wide. Better than expected run defender via leverage and effort. Lack of stride length impact pursuit. Can be handled, strength-wise, one on one against TEs. Still working on hand precision with rush moves.

summary: Standing at 6-foot-6, 285 pounds with good length in his arms and explosiveness out of his stance, those long arms give Stewart an advantage to keep offensive tackles on their heels when he's driving with his legs, but his aiming points with his hands remain high, wide and overall inconsistent. He hasn’t mastered many pass-rush moves and wins mainly off athletic ability right now. When he fires off his front foot in his stance, he can really give offensive tackles trouble to protect their outside shoulder — but he consistently launches off his back foot, which helps them match his speed. He also lets blockers get their hands on him first too often. His anticipation improved in 2024, but he remains a player who often has to see it to react to it. His speed-to-power, specifically from a 3- and 4-point stances is imposing and can really move linemen multiple steps back. He also takes that strong approach to anchoring against the run.
pros_and_cons: Imposing size, even for NFL standards. Top-tier explosiveness at his size. Speed to power can be dominant. Violent hands to disengage. Willing and able to hold the POA against the run. Lets OTs get hands on him first. Pass-rush plans need refinement and more finesse. Hand placement can be wide and off target.

summary: Swinson’s hands are fantastic, whether that be placement and power when stacking or how active and quick they are to stay clean and hit pass-rush moves. He has a good array of pass-rush moves, such as a cross chop, two-hand swipe, and a quick arm- over swim move. His pass-rush win percentage has been exceptionally high for three straight seasons. When engaging to hold the point of attack, his posture can be a bit over his toes and hunched. He also has a bad habit of dropping his eyes. This can cause some balance issues and delays how quickly he can shed blockers after stacking them. Overall, he has very fluid movement skills in both the linear and lateral categories. His movements allow teams to place him in spot-drop zone coverage situations, but his feel and anticipation in coverage need work. He also tends to over pursue misdirection plays in the backfield.
pros_and_cons: Good burst both laterally and linear. Decent speed and bend around the arc. Natural movement skills to drop back into shallow zones. Active hands to hit moves and stay clean when pass rushing. High pass-rush win percentage each of the last three seasons. Hand placement when stacking is good, but slower to shed. Posture is a bit hunched over with weight more on his toes. Has some false/unnecessary steps off the snap.

summary: At 6-foot-4, 270 pounds, he presents good measurables for edge play at the NFL level -- though his arm length does appear to be average or below average. He has a powerful first step and likes to play through contact. He has the flexibility to get low and often makes contact with favorable leverage. He has consistent hand placement for stack and shed in the run game and some fast swipes to stay clean when pass-rushing. He does lack some flexibility to corner and can struggle against offensive tackles with longer arms. His anticipation can be a tick slow at times, but he did play faster and less hesitant in 2024.
pros_and_cons: Powerful first step with few, if any, false steps. Can get low and powerful in pre-snap stance. Strong leg drive that moves OL beyond first contact. Consistent hand placement with good leverage. Fearless to crash down against pulling linemen. Ability to corner is limited due to lack of speed and bend. Anticipation can be a tick slow at times. Can struggle against OTs with long arms.

summary: At just over 6-foot-3 and around 255 pounds, Umanmielen wins with a very impressive first step with some top-tier flexibility and bend. This lends itself to a dip and rip around the outside shoulder and an inside spin move to switch it up — he does both at NFL level. He also has the ability to cross the face of offensive linemen with a nice hesitation move. The rest of his game, however, is a bit erratic. His footwork could be cleaned up. His hands can be fast, but he doesn't use them in a timely manner to keep himself clean when he isn't executing one of his top two moves. He also stays blocked too long. He can be off balance and plays on the ground a bit too much. Though his run-defense grade is strong, that is more from a penetration aspect than an anchoring one.
pros_and_cons: Twitchy player with good at changing directions. Naturally and effectively gets across the face of OL. Longer arms than his height indicates. Has the movement skills to spot drop in coverage. Posses the speed to catch RBs from the backside. Footwork could be cleaned up. Needs to be more consistent snap-to-snap. Crashing stunt plays lack speed-to-power push at contact.

summary: He's small at just 6-foot-1, but his basketball background shows up in his style of setting up blockers. His quick and controlled movements enable him to cross up blockers. This familiar movement also makes him confident as a stunt player — crashing and looping. He is able to mitigate some of his length deficiencies with active hands and a second-nature rip move that he adds to basically every pass-rush move he has. His first step is decent and forced blockers at his level of competition to be quick to set up (or he makes them pay). He also does a nice job of consistently attacking the half-man instead of taking on bigger and longer offensive tackle. When he does go to a bull rush, his lack of height enables him to win the leverage battle consistently for a good pop at contact. Though smaller in size and most experienced in a stand-up pass rush position, there likely isn't much versatility for him to play off-ball linebacker in a large role.
pros_and_cons: Shorter stature gives him leverage for power against OTs. Well-filled out frame top to bottom. Quick and explosive in short areas to cross up blockers. Understands how and why to attack the half man. Good first step to dictate reps and force quick decisions by OTs. Shorter legs make for shorter strides up the arc. Easily pushed aside when OL can square him up. Well below average arm length for the NFL.

summary: In his first year at Georgia, he was a reserve LB and special teams player. In his second year, he played some as an inside linebacker, but he had never played inside linebacker. In 2024, he was a roaming box defender. He played anything from inside linebacker to edge, and he lined up in any gap because his explosiveness, strength and body density made him a versatile player. That versatility had its pros — tons of snap experience attacking the line of scrimmage from all angles. However, it has also clouded his scouting profile — anticipation, instincts and technique all show signs of a tweener player who hasn't mastered one position label. His natural athletic and physical gifts lend themselves to pass rush and edge play in the NFL, but his measurables don’t stack up to most NFL edge defenders. As an off-ball linebacker, he is explosive in pursuit but has some lateral stiffness that makes different drop coverages more of a challenge. He spends most of his time standing up as a 3-4 OLB.
pros_and_cons: Natural pass-rusher off the edge. Adequate size to play ILB/OLB in the NFL. Explosive first step in all directions. Powerful upper body to stack blockers at contact punch. Long arms for a 6-foot-2 frame. Does not have a lot of experience/success in coverage. Currently lacks the lateral quickness needed for off-ball LB work. Instincts and anticipation are still a work in progress.

summary: At 6-foot-5, 265 pounds, Williams is an excellent run defender who is as strong as an ox but also possesses good speed-to- power conversion —- even after just his first step. That first step is also on the better side of average for the NFL level. Though he is still mastering pass-rush moves, he has one of the nastiest and most violent club moves and can combine that with an arm- over/swim or rip move that is tough for anyone to handle. His long-arm move also has a ton of potential. He does need to improve his precision and purpose with his hands to get clean — low pass-rush win percentage in his career. He also needs to develop more counters to quickly and cleanly get off blocks if the first move doesn't work. As for his competitive toughness, his motor runs hot at all times, and he is in no way shy when engaging in contact, no matter the assignment.
pros_and_cons: Great build — weight and length are NFL-caliber. Good understanding of the advantages of his arm length. First-step is explosive and can cover a ton of ground. A violent and fast arm-over/swim move when attacking inside. Strong, reliable run defender who can stack blocks/anchor well. Consistently one of the last linemen out of his stance. Hands are active but could be more purposeful and precise. Must develop more counters.

summary: Bassa was a full-time starter in 2023 and 2024 at Oregon. As a former safety, he is a smooth mover at the second level. He has good pursuit speed to the sideline, and as he is pursuing ball carriers, he is always conscious to square his shoulders and remain sound in his tackling technique. Bassa also plays with an attitude; his competitive toughness will never be in question. He is a constant communicator in the middle of the defense. His top speed is better than his twitch in terms of stop-and-start ability and first-step explosiveness. His smaller size does make it more difficult to get off blocks, but he often makes it so blockers can't line him up. For NFL defenses that don't mind a smaller coverage linebacker, Bassa is a very intriguing player, especially if he can improve his anticipation even more to make up for the lack of twitch.
pros_and_cons: Good athlete who is assigned slot coverage duties versus TEs. Fast to the sideline, but keeps shoulders square when tackling. Plays with an attitude (in a good way). Constant communicator. Advanced feel/ability in coverage with safety background. Slender build could get picked on by pulling linemen. Doesn’t have top-tier twitch when changing direction.

summary: Campbell has major height and length advantages for the position. His height allows him to scan the trenches and backfield, while his long arms can get into passing lanes for PBUs, knock passes away at the catch point, stay clean and hit pass-rush moves when blitzing and punch the ball out across the body when tackling. Speaking of, those long arms have also yielded very low missed tackle numbers over the last two years. He lacks some true off-ball linebacker instincts and anticipation, but that makes sense given he's only played the position full-time for two seasons. His linear and lateral movements are excellent. This gives him some eye-popping coverage reps in man and zone. Though his listed weight is right around the 50th percentile for the position, there are times when you'd like for him to play with more power. He can also lack some violence to his game, but that feels more due to being patient and controlled rather than a lack of ability to convert speed into power.
pros_and_cons: Ideal size and length for an off-ball backer at the NFL level. Long strides make pursuit a breeze. Viable speed-rush option as a pass-rushing OLB. Long arms for batted passes and pass breakups. Low missed tackle percentage. Anticipation is still a tick slow for where the ball is going. Still developing that "feel" in coverage. Could play with a bit more urgency/at a higher speed.

summary: Carter was one of three linebackers in the Power Five that year to earn 75.0-plus grades as a run defender, pass-rusher and in coverage. While his grades dipped in the following two seasons (70.6 in 2023 and 68.0 in 2024), there are still plenty of reasons to like him in this linebacker class. He's a versatile defender with the ability to succeed in coverage from any alignment, thanks to his range. Carter's biggest issues are his lack of physicality as an undersized linebacker at 6 feet, 231 pounds.
pros_and_cons: Good instincts in zone coverage. Has the range and athleticism to succeed in coverage. Diagnoses plays quickly and gets in positions to make plays. A violent and fast arm-over/swim move when attacking inside. Has been an impactful pass rusher over last three seasons. Undersized player. Has issues stacking and shedding blocks. Tackling issues need to be addressed.

summary: Though he will be one of the older prospects in the class, Knight is close to a finished product. He brings adequate size for linebacker play in the NFL at 6-foot-2 and 245 pounds. He frequently aligns in the middle of South Carolina's defense and has good size to take on pulling linemen and finish tackles (low missed tackle percentage). He is also a fast processor and always seems to be one of the first to take a step in the right direction. His movement skills are very good and appear NFL- caliber. He can flip his hips with natural movements as a ball carrier from his days on offense, and his first step, as well as his top speed, are well above average. These movement skills yielded high coverage scores this past season. He is also a highly competitive player whose motor and toughness will never be in question. His all-out playstyle does come with overaggressive pursuit angles at times.
pros_and_cons: Adequate size for off-ball LB work. Strong tackler with a low missed tackle percentages. Fast processor. Explosive first step, great top speed and a natural lateral mover. Fast hands give him some pass rush potential as a blitzer. All-out play style yields overaggressive angles to the ball. Will be one of the oldest prospects in the class.

summary: The Georgia native saved his best for last as a senior with a career-best 72.4 PFF grade. As his recruiting profile would suggest, Mondon is a gifted athlete with top-notch explosiveness and good speed for the position. He combines that with excellent tackling technique that makes him a dangerous player downhill. That burst and technique are needed because he's not the strongest player right now. Mondon's ability to diagnose plays is still a work in progress as well.
pros_and_cons: Elite explosiveness. Good speed means he has no issues sticking with tight ends. Fantastic tackler — 98th percentile since 2023. Below-average size for the position. Processing speed lags behind right now. Concerning injury history missing four games in 2024.

summary: Paul’s 87.2 PFF grade ranked seventh among all FBS linebackers, and he was one of three who posted 78.0-plus grades in run-defense, coverage and as a pass-rusher. He's a fluid and explosive player who rarely misses tackles. Paul's biggest issues are his lack of length and strength, which show up most when he's taking on blocks. He projects as an impact special-teamer while he adds weight to his frame.
pros_and_cons: Fluid athlete allowing him to make plays sideline-to-sideline. Outstanding tackler missing only 6.2% of attempts since 2023. Weapon as a blitzer, explosive downhill. Excellent communicator pre-and-post snap. Very undersized. His lack of size shows up when attempting to shed blocks. Not as good in tight spaces as he is in open field.

summary: Schwesinger is light for NFL standards at 6-foot-2 and 225 pounds (242 at combine). However, he plays like he weighs 240. He gives defenses everything he has on every snap but doesn't do so recklessly — his motor runs hot, but his discipline and fundamentals remain. Despite only one year as a starter, he shows elite processing speed and understanding of the game. His pursuit speed is adequate for the NFL level, and his vision to the ball carrier is top tier. His quickness, combined with his processing, is where he shines. Because of how controlled and agile he is, there is not a lot of separation created against him when using misdirection and play-action. This also aids him in his pass-rush reps. His lack of mass does show up when taking on pulling OL, and he can get blocked up against tight ends one-on- one. However, he does not shy away from the physical requirements of playing the position, even in those situations.
pros_and_cons: Pursuit speed and vision are NFL-caliber. Controlled footwork to not bite versus misdirection/play action. Consistently has his shoulders square to the ball/defenders. Is not shy for physical play despite lower weight profile. Consistent wrap-up effort and discipline. Lighter weight gets him in trouble against pullers/climbing OL. Lacks density, so he needs to wrap up to bring players down.

summary: Simon is a traditional inside linebacker who is most comfortable between the tackles. His run fits are sound, and he generally is where he has to be to impact the game. He has high coverage grades from defending running backs in the flat, but his coverage grade drops significantly when asked to perform more difficult coverage responsibilities. He is a smaller linebacker in terms of weight, which shows up when taking on blocks. He also appears to have shorter arms than average, which affects how well he gets off blocks and wraps up ball carriers. He could stand to play with more violence at contact, but he does do it occasionally. He does have a nice first step and some quick movements but lacks some long speed to be a difference-making pursuit player. He does have some slipperiness between offensive linemen when blitzing the A and B gaps.
pros_and_cons: Traditional between-the-tackle linebacker. Good feel for run defense. Sound between his gaps. Lower weight profile shows up when trying to disengage blocks. Could be more violent when taking on blocks. Seems to have shorter arms than average.

summary: The former four-star recruit's calling card is his run defense, as he leads all Power Four linebackers in stops and tackles for loss/no- gain over the last couple of seasons. Stutsman's football intelligence shows up in that respect, as does his excellent athletic gifts. However, the opposite is true for him in coverage. He's often a step behind there, whether it be because he recognized a route concept in zone too slowly or an inability to change directions and stick with his receiver in man coverage.
pros_and_cons: Elite run defender who recognizes concepts pre-and-post snap. Very good at stacking and shedding blocks. Good size and speed for the position. Effective blitzer up the middle. Awareness in coverage is subpar so is often a tick late to react. Struggles flipping his hips in coverage. Just an average tackler in his career.

summary: Alexander originally committed to Southeastern Louisiana, the only school to keep its scholarship offer to him after a broken collarbone cost him his senior season of sports in high school. He played with the Lions for three seasons and was an FCS All- American in his sophomore campaign and a two-time all- conference selection. Alexander then transferred to LSU but tore his ACL after starting eight games. He returned for 2024 as a full- time starter once again. He is a smart, fluid mover, but does seem to lack NFL-level top speed and explosiveness for the position. Though he has the length and fundamentals to play in press-man coverage, limited athleticism can get him in trouble. He had consistent ball production throughout all five years of his college career. He is reliable as a tackler and dependable in run defense.
pros_and_cons: Experienced man coverage defender. Anticipates movements from press well. Can read receivers’ eyes and anticipate with his back turned. Willing tackler with a very low missed tackle rate. Experience hand-fighting and disrupting receivers' routes. Not the most explosive or twitchy athlete in the class. Could clean up footwork. Top speed vs. vertical receivers is not great.

summary: In addition to football, Amos was a standout in track and field in high school, running the 100-meter and 200-meter dashes and winning the state title in the long jump. He committed to Louisiana-Lafayette and played there for three seasons before transferring to Alabama in 2023 and Ole Miss in 2024. Amos has ideal size for a cornerback — better-than-50th percentile numbers in height, weight and length. This allows him to play press-man coverage with quick footwork and sound hand technique at the line of scrimmage. He can also play off-zone coverage. He does some of his best work from Cover 3 and quarters schemes. He notched just four interceptions in five years (three in 2024), but he recorded a forced incompletion percentage above 20% in each of the past three seasons. His enthusiasm for tackling can run hot and cold, but he is generally a good wrap-up tackler and understands his assignment in run fits.
pros_and_cons: Good athlete in all facets with a multi-sport background. Very high forced incompletion rates over past three seasons. Great coverage instincts. Likes to get hands on receivers and be physical to stay on them. Good strength to rip off WR blocks. Top speed won't "wow" you despite sprinter background. Tendency to tackle high.

summary: Barron, a four-star recruit, was a wide receiver, defensive back and punt returner in high school. He also ran track, recording a personal-best 10.95 in the 100-meter dash. He began his Texas career at safety before moving to more of a nickel role in 2023 and then started as a wide cornerback in 2024. The 5-foot-11, 195-pound defensive back has a ton of versatility. He is well built and athletic, and he tackles and defends the run well enough to start as a safety, as a nickel or out wide. He brings excellent instincts, anticipation and spatial awareness in zone to make plays on the ball or warrant no-throws. He was often running in- breaking routes for receivers before they broke on their route. Despite his track background, Barron doesn't have the best long speed, which is why he shines brightest in zone assignments off the line. He plays with the right amount of competitive toughness. Texas put a ton on his plate, and he always rose to the occasion.
pros_and_cons: Adequate size and strength for run defense/tackling from slot. Good closing speed. Very good feel for spot zone coverage. Good eyes and anticipation no matter where he is lined up. Versatility for any DB spot. Hips a little slower to flip to match route breaks. Can get uncomfortable when his back is to the ball. Gets handsy if he doubts his speed in a situation.

summary: Bowman was four-star recruit coming out of Denton, Texas and chose to play at Oklahoma over Alabama, Texas and others. He saw playing time immediately with the Sooners, starting seven games as a true freshman. While spending the majority of his career at free safety, Bowman has also seen 500-plus snaps both in the box and as a slot corner. His evaluation is a fairly simple one. Bowman is one of the best ball-hawks in this class thanks to his elite combination of range, ball skills and instincts. On the other hand, he's missed over a quarter of his career tackle attempts due to a lack of length and his slight frame.
pros_and_cons: Outstanding ball skills and instincts. Elite speed. Versatility to man up in the slot or play centerfield at free safety. Powerful upper body to stack blockers at contact punch. Long arms for a 6-foot-2 frame. Undersized to be a true safety. Has had major issues over his career bringing down ballcarriers. Big-bodied receivers can box him out in contested situations.

summary: Bryant, who is indeed named after the late NBA legend Kobe Bryant, was a full-time starter at Kansas over the past three seasons. At 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, he is near the lowest weight percentile for an NFL cornerback. Yet, how he plays the game makes him impossible to write off. Beyond his good movement skills and plus arm length, Bryant is a top-tier competitor. He plays with an attitude you want from a defensive back. He yearns to be physical and is comfortable hand-fighting to disrupt and annoy receivers. This can get him in trouble with penalties, but it has its pros, too. He has ideal ball skills, notching multiple interceptions in every year of his college career. His feet and change-of-direction speed are slower than ideal, which likely limits him to off-zone coverage roles to keep things in front of him and downhill. His long speed appears average for the position. Despite his smaller and slender frame, he is a competitive run defender and tackler.
pros_and_cons: Fiery competitor. Will run at tackles full speed with a hitter's mentality. Playmaker who wants to make the biggest play, every play. Closing speed in off coverage is good enough to jump passes. Long arms to get hands on receivers and disrupt catch point. Very slender build limits how well he can wrap up tackles. High-waisted build makes change of direction less sharp. Aggressive mentality can get him in trouble.

summary: Burke missed all but one game in his senior high school season due to a dislocated shoulder, but that didn't stop him from making an immediate impact at Ohio State, as he started 11 games as a true freshman. He went on to start in every season of his four- year career with the Buckeyes. He's a natural mover and has plenty of experience in man and zone, but his skill sets lend themselves to a zone-heavy scheme in the NFL. That’s because of his lack of long speed/recovery speed. When Burke can space himself in off coverage correctly, he can mitigate his lack of long speed with some savvy bump-and-run coverage. If he can't dictate the route with good physicality in press, he can get beat over the top too easily. He put himself in good positions to make tackles but wasn't a reliable finisher in college. He was more reliable in 2024, though. Burke recorded just four interceptions in his career, but his forced incompletion rate was high across his first three seasons.
pros_and_cons: Natural, smooth mover. Good eyes in zone. Good feel for spacing to bait throws/warrant no throws. Willing to be in position in run defense. High forced incompletion rate despite lack of INTs. Feet can be a tick slow to mirror out of press. Top speed is average so, he can get grabby against faster WRs. Instincts and anticipation are still a work in progress.

summary: Dotson was named a second-team All-American at Kansas in 2024. He has a good build, ranking above the 50th percentile in height and length, though he is around the 40th percentile in weight. He has a good understanding of technique and spacing and can stop to change direction and trigger downhill at an adequate pace for the NFL. His arm length yielded a decent forced incompletion rate over the past two years, with multiple interceptions in each of the past three seasons. He has decent strength for run defense and tackling, though getting off blocks can be a struggle. He has suitable movement skills but leaves room for receivers to separate; he's never too far away, but he isn't as sticky as you want. Dotson is smooth in his backpedals and shuffle technique, which helps him stay close to receivers and lends itself to him playing in press man. While his teammate Cobee Bryant did most of the talking in Kansas’ cornerback group, Dotson was more of a silent killer.
pros_and_cons: Good twitch and change-of-direction movement ability. Nice recovery speed. Keeps his shoulders square when lining up tackles. Oily hips. Good stop-and-start control and explosiveness. Can get pushed off the line in press against bigger receivers. Foot speed could be faster, more precise and ready to explode.

summary: Fortune arrived at South Carolina as a safety but moved to cornerback in his redshirt season. He played as a rotational cornerback over the following two years before becoming a full- time starter in 2023 and 2024. He has a long, athletic build at over 6 feet. That length and strength help him disrupt the catch point in close coverage. He has a slender build but brings good pound- for-pound strength. Despite his safety background, he is an inconsistent tackler in timing and technique. He lacks the overall long speed and hip fluidity for press-man coverage. Fortune is more experienced, controlled and effective as an off-zone cornerback, primarily in Cover 3. He brought in nine interceptions over the past three seasons but recorded a low forced incompletion rate as a starter. That seems to stem from a lack of stickiness in single coverage over a lack of ball skills (he is a pretty natural catcher). He also consistently has his eyes on punching the ball out.
pros_and_cons: Ideal length (height and arms) for the NFL. Good length to disrupt the catch point when close in coverage. Always has his eyes on punching the ball out. Lateral movements are good for a player of his size. High missed tackle percentages in each of past three seasons. Currently lacks the lateral quickness needed for off-ball LB work. Anticipation needs to be a bit quicker for zone coverage.

summary: Hairston became a full-time starting cornerback in 2023 at Kentucky and missed a good chunk of 2024 with a shoulder injury. Mad Max, as he is nicknamed, has a quick play style that makes for a fun watch. He is a constant pre- and post- snap communicator and also gets verbal with wide receivers throughout the game. His height and length appear to be average for the position, but his 180-pound weight profile ranks in the single-digit percentiles (8th). Hairston’s hands are active in press, at the catch point and through the route. His interception total in 2023 stemmed more from bad throws, but his forced incompletion rate was above 10% over the past two seasons. He brings a feisty play style that, of course, can lead to penalties. He is one of the more explosive cornerbacks in the draft with some of the best top speed in the class.
pros_and_cons: Solid wrap-up tackler. Visible communicator pre- and post-snap. Shows a good understanding of run-fit duties. Adequate first-step quickness and acceleration. Very light build. Hands get grabby when he’s in trouble. Lacks true anticipation and can look of control at times.

summary: Hill committed to Arizona State but transferred to Nebraska after one season. He played as a full-time outside cornerback in 2024 but missed most of the year due to plantar fasciitis. Hill plays a physical brand of football. He knows he brings plus size for the position at over 6 feet and 210 pounds. He is a bit clunky when flipping his hips out of press and looks more natural in off coverage. He has the physical profile to play man but lacks the savviness to do so. His best work comes in zone assignments where he can keep things in front and come downhill. Because of his build, Hill is a strong run defender and tackler, making it tempting to put him closer to the line of scrimmage. He has some fluidity stiffness, so a move to safety could be in his NFL future, but he did not play there much in college. Despite his receiver background, he didn’t have much ball production outside of 2023. His overall athleticism seems good, but it’s hard to see it at all times.
pros_and_cons: Massive measurements for an outside cornerback. Good baseline of natural movement skills. Strong player, given his build. Shows flashes of good anticipation for breaking on the ball. Good understanding of spacing/leverage. Not super comfortable in straight backpedal from press. Footwork is clunky out of press. Athleticism could be lacking for the NFL.

summary: The No. 1 overall recruit in the 2022 class, Hunter is a legitimate NFL starter at cornerback and wide receiver. He lived up to the hype as the Heisman Trophy winner and a consensus All- American in 2024. His profile starts with a rare playmaker's mentality. Hunter’s long, lean frame gives him plus length at cornerback. His feet move fast, and his first-step explosiveness is very good to break on passes. He has the best ball skills of any defensive back I have ever scouted. He has good instincts in space but can get erratic, stemming from a desire to make a big play. His frame is lighter, leading to some strength and tackling deficiencies, but it looks like he can put on good weight in the NFL. His movements out of press-man coverage can be out of control. Playing him more in off-coverage zone allows him to hawk the ball and limit missteps. He also has plenty of talent to play man coverage. Most negatives feel like nitpicking, as Hunter boasts an All-Pro ceiling.
pros_and_cons: Impressive top speed/recovery speed. Height/length is a big plus in press coverage. Some of the best ball skills you'll ever see in a DB. Knack for baiting QBs and making them pay in zone. Elite zone coverage player in every way. Foot speed can be delayed due to longer legs. Lack of weight shows up when tackling and hand-fighting. Can be a bit out of control at times.

summary: Johnson earned five starts in 2022 as a true freshman before starting 11 games in Michigan's national championship campaign in 2023. He missed most of his 2024 season due to a severe case of turf toe, as well as a minor shoulder injury. The 6-foot-2, 200-pound outside cornerback has some of the quickest feet you will see. Though his limited long speed makes zone schemes his best fit, he can play press-man due to how quick he is to stop, start and change direction. His long arms come in handy for forced incompletions, a number that was near the 55th percentile over the past two years. His frame is leaner and lighter, but he still shows decent effort in run defense. Strength and tackling aren't his strong suits, though, and he was even more inconsistent there in 2024. When Johnson keeps his eyes on the quarterback in off-zone coverage, he has good instincts to jump routes and bait throws, as evidenced by his nine interceptions and three pick-sixes in college.
pros_and_cons: Change-of-direction ability is that of a much smaller corner. Versatile to play on left or right side. Very good understanding of leverages. Smooth when passing off receivers and picking them up in zone. Fluid transitions from backpedal to shuffle to full stride. Some inconsistent/ineffective timing with punches in press. Top speed is good, but doesn't appear to be great with recovery. Sloppy with tackling attempts in 2024.

summary: Longerbeam is a fast, explosive athlete, but he currently weighs only 175 pounds. He plays bigger than his size in coverage, and the vast majority of his college snaps came at outside cornerback. Longerbeam can frequently put himself in a good enough position in zone coverage to read the quarterback and impact coverage zones outside of his own. His tremendous foot quickness makes him a sticky red-zone coverage player. He has the long speed to stay with bigger wide receivers in press coverage. Longerbeam also has a knack for making plays on the ball, tallying two interceptions and nine pass breakups in 2024. He will need to add some weight and strength, but his quick feet, deep speed and long arms are a valuable combination.
pros_and_cons: Elite change-of-direction ability. Very good recovery speed. Long arms come into play at the catch point. Timed physicality at the catch point to prevent completions. Will overrun the ball carrier on run plays. Thin frame can get pushed around by run blockers. Peeks at the QB for too long and get beat deep in off coverage.

summary: Morrison started nine games as a true freshman at Notre Dame and then started 11 the following season. He was a full-time starter again in 2024 but missed a good chunk of the Irish's national championship run due to a hip injury that shouldn't affect him long term. He has a long, lean frame at 6 feet and around 190 pounds. That’s evident in his very high forced incompletion rate (20.5%) over the past two seasons. His short-area movements are explosive yet fluid, which allows him to play press-man coverage, mirror releases inside or out and transition from backpedal to full strides seamlessly. Morrison’s lean frame does come with drawbacks. While he is a willing and smart run defender, he lacks the strength to be a great tackler or to get off blocks quickly. He also may lack true long speed and can get grabby with receivers if they can stack him vertically. He is praised for his high football IQ and maturity, even as a true junior entering the draft.
pros_and_cons: Appears to have very long arms, even for a 6-footer. Hands are up and active in press. Quick to transition from shuffle to full strides. Good awareness for getting his head around to find the ball. Very high football IQ. Strength is a concern with getting off blocks and tackling. Start-stop ability is good, especially for his size, but not top-tier. Can get grabby to stick with WRs on comeback routes.

summary: Parrish is a former three-star cornerback recruit from Olathe, Kansas. At Olathe North High School, he played receiver, defensive back and even running back and set the school record for receiving yards. He was also a standout track athlete, winning the state title in the 100m with a time of 10.47 seconds. After playing as a rotational member of the secondary as a true freshman in 2022, he became a full-time starter in 2023 and 2024. He is smaller in stature but a feisty competitor. His best projection is as a slot defender, where his body control and short- area explosiveness can shine. His track background gives him outstanding recovery speed. Against bigger receivers, Parrish tends to get overly physical. While he can sometimes be an ankle-biter as a tackler, he gives strong effort and shows high football IQ when fitting the run. He is most confident in press-man coverage from the slot and consistently stuck to receivers' hips at the college level.
pros_and_cons: Impressive acceleration and top speed despite short strides. Fluid and fast footwork. Strong body control to stop and start efficiently. Consistently dives at ankles when tackling. Needs to be more subtle with contact at receivers' break points. Good body control, but feet slide out from under him too often.

summary: Porter committed to Iowa State as a wide receiver and played mostly on special teams before moving to cornerback in 2022. His primary role remained special teams until 2024, when he was a full-time starter. He is a rare prospect in many ways. The first is his elite track background, which gives him great explosiveness and recovery speed. The second is his measurables, with his height and arms ranking above the 95th percentile. He didn’t have much time to showcase his ball skills, but he has great hands. His build is on the slender side, and though the effort is there, he lacks strength in multiple areas — mainly tackling and getting off blocks. His lack of experience has led to clunkiness in his backpedals and a lack of anticipation for receiver movements and punch timing. Porter is at his best when he can play off the line of scrimmage in zone and close downhill faster than the offense expects. He blocked five kicks in college: four punts and one field goal.
pros_and_cons: Very alluring length. Elite recovery speed and acceleration. Really smooth and natural mover, given his height and length. Receiver background makes him a natural at the catch point. Takes on blocks and funnels ball carriers back inside. Does not have much experience as a starting CB. Handled fairly easily against pulling blockers in run defense. Lacks anticipation, especially when approaching to tackle.

summary: Ransaw is a former two-star cornerback recruit from Harvest, Alabama, where he played defensive back and served as a returner at Sparkman High School. He spent three seasons at Troy before transferring to Tulane for his final year of college football. In the two seasons where he saw the most playing time, he primarily lined up as a nickel defender. His strengths stem from his plus size, tackling power and reliability. He posted a very low missed tackle percentage in each of the last two seasons. He likes to use his length to get his arms up and bump receivers in man coverage, but his anticipation is lacking. His footwork can be sluggish in press, often putting him in recovery mode. Although he tested as an elite athlete at the combine, that athleticism doesn’t always translate into big plays on the field. His best NFL position may be as a downhill safety, where he wouldn’t be tasked with covering quick slot receivers and could instead maximize his tackling ability.
pros_and_cons: Strong run defender with good play strength. Very low missed tackle percentage throughout his career. Not as fast as his Combine numbers would suggest. Lacks anticipation, limiting the effectiveness of his athleticism. Slow feet off the line of scrimmage.

summary: Revel transferred to East Carolina in 2022 and played in nine games before becoming a full-time starter in 2023. He began the 2024 season as a starter before tearing his ACL in the third game. At 6-foot-3, Revel brings ideal height and length to the position. He has a slender build, which impacts his effectiveness in tackling and getting off blocks, but he shows no hesitancy in either situation. His athleticism is rare, even independent of his size. His recovery speed and explosiveness are both top-tier. He possesses rare nuance and technique. As a press-man cornerback, he can mirror and stick with any receiver. But he can get lost in space in off-zone coverage. Revel’s punch timing and hand placement in press can also be inconsistent, leading to him playing catch-up more than dictating routes (which works for him because his recovery athleticism is elite). He brings strong forced incompletion production but few interceptions due to a lack of coordination.
pros_and_cons: Very explosive athlete, especially for his size. Top speed will be in the top percentile. Willing and physical run defender. Footwork is fast enough to match WR movements. Bully in press coverage. Explosive, but out of control at times. Anticipation and spacing are still inconsistent. Has the strength to get off blocks, but needs to get clean faster.

summary: Riley committed to Middle Tennessee State out of high school and played there for three seasons before transferring to Louisville. He was a two-year starter with more than 1,500 snaps played in 2023 and 2024. He is a smaller cornerback, placing below the 50th percentile in all measurables, but he makes up for it with twitchiness in his movements. Riley lacks the instincts and feel to really stick with receivers, whether that be in press man or off coverage, though he is best in man. He notched 17 career interceptions and a high forced incompletion rate in college. His biggest negatives are evident when he has to be physical. Even when he puts his whole body into tackles, ball carriers bounce off him. He has a hard time getting off all blocks and can get erased by pullers. His skill set and movements lend themselves more to the slot, but he doesn’t defend the run well enough to play there.
pros_and_cons: Versatile to play left and right CB. Comfortable in man or zone, confident in press. Overall athleticism is adequate. Flashes of good effort in run defense. Impressive ball skills with 17 career INTs. Can get lost in Cover 3 with blind spots. Stays close on comebacks but lacks true stickiness in coverage. Struggles with faster receivers vertically.

summary: Strong committed to Virginia Tech out of the 2020 class and was a consistent starter over the past four years when healthy. He has good height and length at just under 6-foot-1 with just over 31- inch arms. He does have a slender build, and his sub-180 weight ranks in the 6th percentile. He lacks the strength to get off blocks and is generally an unreliable run defender. However, he was a much-improved tackler in 2024. Although he has experience in press, his lack of strength causes issues with punches off the line and hand-fighting. Those weaknesses are mitigated more in an off-quarters/Cover 3 shell. Strong is good at giving receivers the appropriate amount of space to make quarterbacks hesitate. He also knows his closing and recovery speed well; though both are good, they are not elite. His foot quickness is a plus. His receiver background helped him record seven career interceptions and a forced incompletion rate above 13.0% in all five years.
pros_and_cons: Receiver background shows up at the catch point. Quickness and foot speed are adequate for the NFL. Nice feel for Cover-3 assignments. Much more confident as a tackler in 2024. Very competitive. Tough for him to get off blocks to fit the run. Isn't as comfortable in press. Punch technique/timing is inconsistent.
