summary: Thomas brings ideal length to the cornerback position with 85th- percentile arms. He uses those well and effectively at the line of scrimmage in press coverage with massive hands that can really knock receivers off their routes and out of their releases. His overall athleticism is good, but his foot quickness is his calling card. He can sometimes be late or slow with his footwork out of press, which forces him into recovery mode early, but he usually makes up for it. With his receiver background, he has a good feel for where the ball is when in flight, even with his back turned. He is also impactful in Cover 3 roles in a shuffle technique in off coverage. Thomas is a highly competitive player but does lack some strength when getting off blocks and tackling. He will be just 20 years old on draft day and 21 in his rookie season.
pros_and_cons: Constant pre-snap communicator. Punch in press can really jolt receivers back. Competitiveness is evident every game. Good baseline of instincts in man and zone that can get better. Appears to process the game at a high level. Can get taken for a ride vs. pulling blockers and tight ends. Doesn't have rare stop-and-start ability for a longer cornerback. Slender build could use more weight. Shows when tackling.

summary: At 6-foot-1 and 195 pounds, Williams has the size for press coverage assignments. It also happens to be where he is most comfortable and confident. He likes to be physical in how he covers receivers. He wants to dictate contact right at the snap with good, strong hands out of the receiver's release. He is comfortable hand-fighting all the way through the route, but that can get him in trouble, as he can get a bit grabby, especially against vertical routes. Williams’ long speed is likely average for the NFL, and his feet and hips are a bit heavy when changing direction. He has a lot of career interceptions (15), but his forced incompletion rate was still below 15% in each of the past two seasons. He is a reliable tackler with good run-defense instincts and strength.
pros_and_cons: Sense of confidence when the ball is coming his way. Feels at home when there's contact with the receiver. Good ball skills from receiver background. Consistently high run-defense grades over his career. Low and loaded in his shuffle to step and accelerate at any time. Feet could be a bit lighter off the line. Less consistency in off-zone coverage. Tackling form can be up and down.

summary: Clark has a low margin for error due to his lack of recovery speed, so his movements must be precise and well thought out, but they generally are. He lacks the rare athletic ability to be a full-time NFL single high safety, but his anticipation and body placement allow him to be impactful in two-high shells. In the slot, you don't want him playing off coverage, but when lined up against bigger receivers, such as tight ends, he is comfortable getting his hands on them to remain sticky. He is an excellent tackler with good strength and fundamentals for a relatively low missed tackle percentage. He has good ball skills with five interceptions. He plays the game with a strong competitiveness and is willing to do any assignment the safety position may bring.
pros_and_cons: Sound tackler with good technique. Quick footwork in his backpedal form a free safety spot. Extensive experience and football intelligence show up. Highly competitive player. Good ball skills. Doesn't possess top speed for full-time single high work. Acceleration when triggering is below average.

summary: Emmanwori’s elite size and speed combination will undoubtedly draw evaluators’ attention, as he possesses numerous tools that are proven assets at the NFL level. However, his stiffness and lack of anticipation leave him playing catch-up often. He tends to grab receivers and is most effective as a box/slot defender who can match up with tight ends, where his tools work to his advantage. He can get washed down in the run game and over run ball carriers.
pros_and_cons: Size and length are elite, freakish athletic testing. Effective playing in the box/slot/near the line of scrimmage. Makes good use of range paired with ball skills. Flashes makeup speed to undercut crossing routes. Arm tackler in open space led to misses. Stiff hips make life harder on himself. Bailed out from poor reads/recognition by his length and speed. Gets handsy when late to react or behind.

summary: Mukuba transferred from Clemson to Texas for his senior season, and while his three years of starting experience certainly helped, the fact he thrived in a new system with new coaches makes his field command in 2024 all the more impressive. He can transition out of his pedal in a flash and cover a ton of ground, allowing him to make plays on the ball and take aggressive angles in pursuit. He consistently tracks the ball in the air efficiently without compromising his defensive positioning, recording six picks and a 25% forced incompletion rate in 2024. Mukuba’s biggest concern is tackling. His frame looks slight, and his game lacks physicality. While he uses his natural athleticism and instincts to get in position, he tends to leave his feet and tackle with his arms, causing him to fall off too many attempts in the open field. He can still win with pure explosiveness, but there are concerns about his ability to play the run in the box or blitz.
pros_and_cons: Fluid change of direction and top-end speed in space. Decisive/explosive click-and-close ability. Consistently demonstrates a command of his role. Plays the ball in the air, not the receiver. Flashes range and closing burst needed to take strong angles. Slight build. Misses too many tackles by ankle-biting. Lack of physicality also shows up on limited pass rush reps.

summary: Ransom played a pivotal role in Ohio State’s championship run in 2024, providing the Buckeyes defense with a tone-setter on the back end. He's a disruptive force in the run game, where he earned the highest grade (93.5) in the nation thanks to his penchant for punching the ball loose. However, missed tackles litter his tape. His instincts are strong, but he can lack the tools (speed/burst) to execute at times.
pros_and_cons: Has tenacity and physicality in spades. Trusts his instincts and is always around the ball. Delivers hits with authority and is disruptive over the middle. Downhill aggressor playing the run. Always looking to punch out the football. Trouble mirroring breaks. Has middling burst to make up ground. Doesn’t possess high-end speed to match vertically.

summary: Starks is a former five-star athlete recruit and was an instant starter at Georgia in his true freshman season. He earned first- team All-American honors as a sophomore in 2023. He is smaller for a safety, likely slightly below the 50th percentile in height and weight. He has smooth movement skills that allow him to play as a free safety, strong safety and slot defender. As a free safety, his range is good but not elite. His best coverage plays come more from anticipation than incredible top speed. As a strong safety and slot defender, he is a very reliable tackler. As a slot, he is fluid enough to play man coverage against many types of receivers but lacks the elite twitchiness to be a true shutdown slot. Starks’ ball skills are top-tier, and he has some of the most impressive interceptions you'll see from a safety. His play in 2024 dipped due to worse judgment and anticipation, for whatever reason.
pros_and_cons: Lower weight, but a well-built safety. Long wingspan for pass breakups. Top speed is very impressive (sprinter background). Smooth, fluid hips to maximize range in deep coverage. Elite ball skills. Movements can look out of control at times. Can be a little too aggressive in his pursuit angles. Judgment was significantly off in 2024.

summary: Watts, listed as a wide receiver coming out of high school and having played there in his freshman season for the Fighting Irish, unsurprisingly has the best ball skills of any safety in this draft. He picked off 13 passes over the past two seasons; no other defender in the nation had more than nine in that span. While his hands obviously helped with that, it’s his anticipation and intelligence that put him in position to make plays on the ball. The main drawback in Watts’ game is his tackling, though he doesn’t lack physicality. He too often takes bad angles to the ball carrier and plays too off-balance, though he did improve in his fifth and final season. Watts is a versatile coverage defender who can thrive at free safety, in the slot or in the box.
pros_and_cons: Great hands and always in the right place to make plays. High-IQ player with quick twitch. Outstanding when asked to cover man to man in 2024. Versatility to cover at free safety, in the slot and in the box. Diagnoses plays pre- and-post snap. Tackling issues, needs to take better angles and stay balanced. Sometimes gets caught flat-footed in coverage. A little stiff when forced to flip his hips and change directions.

summary: A partially torn ACL prematurely ended Winston’s junior season after just two games and thus ended his first-round hype for the draft. However, his sophomore tape in 2023 is good enough to still consider him at the top of this safety class. The Maryland native was the only safety in the nation with 85.0-plus grades as a run defender and in coverage that year. Winston is also as elite as they come as a tackler, missing just two of his 89 career attempts. He’s a very good athlete for the position, as he has fluid hips and sideline-to-sideline range. Truthfully, the only major question mark in his game is how he recovers from his knee injury. If his medicals check out and he still slips into the third round, Winston could become one of the steals of the draft.
pros_and_cons: As good of a tackler as you’ll find in this class. Diagnoses plays pre- and post-snap and make plays on the ball. Was outstanding when asked to cover man-to-man this season. Versatility to cover at free safety, in the slot and in the box. Partially torn ACL ended his junior season after just two games. Only one interception in his career. Reaction time can be a tick behind sometimes.
